The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

What is it? A high-fantasy survival crafting RPG set in the genre's most impressive sandbox. Release date: October 15, 2026 (1.0) Expect to pay: $40/£35 Developer: Keen Games Publisher: Keen Games Reviewed on: RTX 4080, AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 64GB RAM Steam Deck: Verified Link: Steam | Official site

High up on a mountain in the Albaneve Summits, just on the southern border of Enshrouded's new zone, I spot the perfect place for my next medieval building project. It seems safe with no nearby enemy spawns on the flat stretch of land, and there's even a cute frozen pond that gives it real Christmas-card appeal. I love it, and I'll love it even more once I've built a cliffside castle.

The only problem is I can't find a way up by climbing or gliding, so I'll have to make my own. I could build something, but that takes time, and I'm impatient. Instead, I behave like an absolute heathen—I bomb and pickaxe the hell out of the mountainside, carving a tunnel from the base to the top. It doesn't look great, but that's a problem for tomorrow's Flameborn.

That's always been one of my favorite parts of Enshrouded: you can destroy or build practically anything, anywhere in Embervale's voxel-based world. It's a survival crafting sandbox filled to the brim with handcrafted details, and every location still hidden by the fog of war could hold a new material, powerful weapon, or scenic vista. There's nothing quite like it, and just like the updates before, Enshrouded's 1.0 build keeps finding new, inventive ways to impress me long after I thought its well of surprises had run dry.

Enshrouded is a weird one. Not quite a traditional survival crafting game, but not a typical action RPG either. Its combat system and base building options are far more robust than most of its survival crafting cousins, but it's not nearly as brutal. I'm driven less by desperation and more by a desire to explore Embervale—a land devastated by a mysterious, malignant miasma known as (you guessed it) the Shroud. There's hardly a soul left in the world, so you learn more about its history from journals. Some are hastily scribbled by would-be heroes like you, while others are tragic retellings of someone's final days.

A few survivors remain as recruitable NPCs for your base. I love how lively they make player-made homes feel, even if the AI is a bit dopey.

One of my favorite additions in 1.0 is the voiceover added to every journal. The same narrator reads them all, giving the whole thing an endearing storybook feel as he shifts tone and pitch for different authors.

I found my favorite journal in a tiny, mountainside cave left by an old man grieving his wife. You can wander around the surrounding area for more environmental storytelling, but I have to warn you: some details got me teary-eyed.

So, for what must be the millionth time in my career, I stumble out of a mystical, sleepy haze confused and poorly dressed for the world I've awakened to. I am the Flameborn—a sort of ordained-by-god chosen one and the last hope for restoring the ruins of Embervale—but for now, I certainly don't feel that way. I just feel like some guy. It's a title I'll have to grow into, but will have to wait until I've upgraded from the aptly named 'ragged armor set'. Yeesh.

Enshrouded follows most of those rags-to-riches genre basics, so of course I'll graduate from an era of fighting with sticks and eating fistfuls of berries to magic-infused swords and Michelin-star meals. I've played so many of these games that the flow comes naturally now, but what I like most about Enshrouded's take on classic survival systems is that it drops the more punitive elements like fatigue, crafting chance, and even structural integrity.

Enshrouded has a robust set of custom difficulty options, but I learned the hard way to leave them alone until after you've tried the first dungeon.

An early access update added a custom setting for dehydration and starvation, but I much prefer playing without it .

There's cooking, farming, and even animal husbandry. Those systems are compelling enough as is, and don't gain anything by adding do-this-or-die mechanics.

Enshrouded knows that I, much like the family Golden Retriever, am treat-motivated. As long as there's shelter, fire, and decor, I'll get a stamina-boosting buff just by hanging out at home, but I'll never die from lack of sleep. In that regard, it's more like Valheim. Unique furnishings have their own comfort stats too, so there's incentive to explore Embervale for a new rug, fireplace, or even a toilet if you want a longer, more powerful boost. It's an especially exciting system for players like me, someone who loves building and decorating bases, but rarely sees a reward for the extra effort.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

All this meticulous decorating makes me wonder whether I really want Enshrouded to add enemy raids on player bases and risk destroying them, but I'm leaning toward yes. It's the one major survival mechanic I miss in its formula, and I can't help but wistfully remember how fun it is to scramble into action when Valheim warns, "The forest is moving..." Imagine that, but with Enshrouded's poisonous fog instead.

Enshrouded has always been my favorite survival-crafting block set, but I'm thrilled with the new build camera. Building in tight corners is less hassle, and I don't slide off the roof a dozen times..

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd. It's nice to go from picking at scraps to being overwhelmed by choice

Version 1.0 also added Sparkworks, a logic system for creating your own enemy spawns, player-triggered events, special world builds, custom dungeons, and more. Your creations are shareable, too, so other players can suffer through your cruel obstacle course designs. I've tinkered with it myself, but I've mostly spent my time exploring player-made hobbit holes and feeling painfully self-conscious by comparison.

Repetitive tasks—another hunt for a rare material, another trek across the map—can become exasperating even in the best survival crafting games. There's a thin line between tedium and satisfaction, and Enshrouded walks it better than most. Much of that is thanks to the game's philosophy around punishment and reward, but its RPG elements add a layer of complexity that more than makes up for anything missing from Enshrouded's "survival-lite" approach.

Take my group, for example. I play with seven other friends, while that feels like a lot for most survival crafting games, Enshrouded's combat roles give us distinctly useful jobs. Rather than dumping points into three or four barebones stats, your Flameborn can specialize across 12 different skill trees. I mostly opt for tank, athlete, and assassin perks, but my allies fill other needs with mix-and-match builds for glass-cannon wizards, battlemage healers, or stealthy assassins. We also have our preferred responsibilities, like mining, woodcutting, gardening, cooking, and all those other usual genre chores.

Enshrouded's boss fights are a blast and more dynamic than similar games. Fights aren't as mechanically heavy as a Conan Exiles dungeon boss, but the traditional tank-and-spank approach won't cut it.

Hollow Halls—Enshrouded's massive dungeons that practically demand group play—are where combat roles shine the most. I beat one playing solo, but also wiped several times in a group of four.

A word of caution: multiplayer groups of more than two or three people should consider a dedicated server. Version 1.0 significantly improves performance, but not enough to spare bigger parties from the occasional murderous lag spike.

Multiplayer is also where some of my biggest gripes with Enshrouded remain, and despite heavy reworks to its questing systems, my group still struggled to make sense of the journal when our objectives fell out of sync. Our confusion mostly stemmed from completing world progression quests without the full party, so when absent friends logged back in, their to-do list didn't look the same and they had a list of missed quests. There are separate, personal quests to do at your own leisure, but we constantly compared our journals to make sure no one had gone off course.

I'm still not sure if any of that even mattered. No one was ever locked out of crafting recipes or new biomes because of the discrepancies, so the punishment boiled down to a smidge of missed XP and simply missing out on the moment. It didn't end up being a big deal, and I'm starting to think the journal's 'missed quest' label made the whole thing feel more consequential than it actually was. I clenched my jaw in frustration a few times, but if that's my biggest nitpick, then Enshrouded is survival crafting gold.

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd.

As much as I love the genre, I can't pretend it isn't filled with seemingly eternal early access pits. I've played in plenty of messy sandboxes, a handful of good ones, and just a few great ones. Then there's Enshrouded, operating in a league of its own. But even then, Enshrouded isn't just a good survival crafting game: it's a damn good game by any measure. Its building tools reward even my most impractical ambitions, and I'll never grow tired of exploring Embervale's hidden nooks and crannies.

Few games in the genre match its distinct identity or degree of polish, and after 500+ hours of adventuring, there's little left to wish for. My biggest dilemma post-Enshrouded will be moving on from a survival crafting RPG so lovingly handcrafted. I fear Keen Games has cooked up something that has forever changed my palate.

The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

Andrea has been covering games for nearly a decade, picking up bylines at IGN, USA Today, Fanbyte, and Destructoid before joining the PC Gamer team in 2025. She's got a soft spot for older RPGs and is willing to try just about anything with a lovey-dovey "I can fix them" romance element. Her weekly to-do always includes a bit of MMO time, endlessly achievement hunting and raiding in Final Fantasy 14. Outside of those staples, she's often got a few survival-crafting games on rotation and loves a good scare in co-op horror games.

#3843. Sony has snapped up the film rights for Mouthwashing

Sony has snatched up the movie rights for Mouthwashing, the hit independent horror video game released in 2024.

Deadline reports Sony has obtained the rights from developer Wrong Organ and publisher Critical Reflex, and also brought on Karyn Kusama to direct the adaptation, a director perhaps best known for her work on the acclaimed Yellowjackets television show.

Sony has also enlisted Matt Manfredi and Phil Hay to write for the project, as well as production company Crooked Highway (who you may know for the Ethan Hawke–lead series of movies, The Black Phone). There is no word on which actors will star in the adaptation as of yet, nor whether the story will follow that of the game's own narrative.

Mouthwashing was a critically acclaimed release, and sold more than 500,000 copies as of February 2025. That was on PC alone, with the game made available on consoles yesterday.

This adaptation would arguably follow the path paved by the Iron Lung movie, created by Mark Fischbach (better known by his online alias Markiplier) and his own production company Markiplier Studios. That, a film adaptation of an indie horror game, performed exceptionally well at the box office bringing in $21m globally shortly after its premiere.

A Mouthwashing movie is an interesting idea. The main question is whether or not it would follow the plot and narrative structure of the game faithfully, or whether changes would be made to better suit the big screen. A sillier - but awfully tantalising - question, is who you'd like to see casted in the movie? Who'd play Swansea… Who'd play Jimmy?!? Questions abound.

#3842. Delve into "a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors" in the latest Fallout 4 quest mod from the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project

A mysterious bunker with out of this world contents

After adding a whole new town to Fallout 4 last month, a group of modders have released another in their long string of extra quests for the RPG. This latest mission revolves around a dungeon delve in the Glowing Sea, where a mysterious bunker's just been unearthed.

"The harsh radioactive winds of the Glowing Sea have uncovered a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors," the group behind the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project (CSEP) declared the description of this latest work, Under The Stars.

A fresh dungeon with a quest attached, the mod tasks you with donning your hazmat suit for a trip to a sunken bunker in the region of post-apocalyptic Boston with the least chill weather. Inside await voiced holotapes and puzzles offering clues as to what went down in this cosy corner of the Commonwealth, plus some new gear to make braving whatever lurks within worth it.

Spoilers: Judging by the screenshots, it looks like the place is an Area 51-esque hidey-hole for evidence of aliens and other cryptic oddities.

If you're unfamiliar, the CSEP lot are responsible for a bunch of popular Fallout 4 quest mods based around the likes of deadly cults, underground wars, post-apocalyptic detective work, and Brotherhood of Steel drama. While Under The Stars doesn't look have been as big an undertaking as those, that previous form points to it being an expertly-crafted addition that'll slot seamlessly into the game.

The modders have put Under The Stars together as part of a community-hosted modding jam called Fallout Flood, with this latest one based around the theme of being underground. Among the other works to have come out of it thus far are another Fallout 4 quest mod dubbed Stranded - The Oasis, a dungeon full of funky rats called the S'Laven, and a new robot enemy you can wear as a hat. It's also produced a New Vegas quest mod about exploring an abandoned NCR railway, so seems to have been very productive gathering of modding minds.

To give Under The Stars a go, your copy of Fallout 4 will need to have the Automatron and Vault-Tec Workshop DLCs.

#3841. The Division 2 Echoes of Central Park DLC release countdown: Exact date and time

The Echoes of Central Park DLC is coming soon to The Division 2, and we won’t have to wait long to try out the major expansion. Ubisoft has already teased the DLC, which will feature a new map and plenty of new story content for players to explore. First, let’s find out when Central Park becomes available as an in-game region to all of us.

The Echoes of Central Park DLC goes live worldwide on Tuesday, Nov. 3. The release date was announced earlier by the developers, and I am not expecting any change this late. The following countdown will expire once the DLC goes live.

The countdown is based on the following times.

The new DLC allows you to explore Central Park for the first time. The park is now home to a new threat that lurks in the shadows. You’ll not only face them, but also uncover the park’s mystery.

You’ll find three reluctant heroes to guide you through the park. Each ally has a unique gameplay style, so you have the choice of who should accompany you.

Echoes of Central Park also brings a new endgame experience. Once you complete the story, you can return to the location to dictate the fight, pursue enemies, and experience the different modifiers that are at play.

Once you defeat the different enemies present at Central Park, you’ll gain six new skill variants inspired by the same horrors you face. Overall, there’s plenty to experience, whether you’re a veteran or new to the series.

"He was put forth with probably what felt like a very arduous task"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Uncharted 4: A Thief's End marks a high point for the series in terms of emotionally resonant storytelling, capping off a rollicking, action-packed adventure with a surprisingly poignant epilogue showing Nathan Drake's comparatively mundane life as a father 15 years after the events of the main story. I've played that game so many times I've lost count, and the ending never fails to wet my eyes just a little. That's why I was shocked to hear creative director Neil Druckmann put together the rough outline within weeks, according to a developer who was working with him at the time.

Ryan Trowbridge, who was character technical director on Uncharted 2 through 4, tells Kiwi Talkz that Druckmann ran an "efficient" ship at Naughty Dog when he took over as creative director from Amy Hennig, who left the studio abruptly in early 2014 during Uncharted 4's development.

"He was put forth with probably what felt like a very arduous task of 'how do you take this IP and make number four of Uncharted, and breathe more life into it, and keep going, and also take over a project that's already been in production for a while'," says Trowbridge. "And he so quickly took what was there. In my recollection, it seemed like it took him only a couple weeks to regather himself."

Trowbridge says it's possible Druckmann knew about his new role for longer than was apparent, which would've given him more time to prepare a new story for Uncharted 4, "but he went and he had written a new" plot for the game. Druckmann had "adjusted to the story, took advantage of a bunch of things that he had already done, added some other things that he felt were needed, and very quickly got us on track."

Druckmann and game director Bruce Straley definitely had big shoes to fill in the wake of Hennig's departure, which itself sparked major controversy when IGN reported that Druckmann and Straley forcibly removed Hennig from the project. Naughty Dog immediately denied that claim and it was officially retracted by IGN years later, but Druckmann's role as successor to Hennig on Uncharted 4 remains one of the most controversial topics in the Naughty Dog pantheon to this day. The fact that the game itself is nothing short of a gameplay and narrative triumph is a testament to Druckmann and Straley's perseverance in the face of intense scrutiny.

#3839. Forza director, who'd been with Turn 10 for 27 years leaves Microsoft, following studios merger with Playground Games

Dan Greenawalt, director, founder, and vice president at Turn 10 Games, has departed from the studio after spending 27 years as part of the company. This comes as Turn 10 is merged with Playground Games as part of Xbox's mass restructuring initiative that made headlines as it resulted in 3200 layoffs and four studio closures earlier this year.

In a report by The Verge, an internal memo written by Playground Games studio head Trevor Williams states: "Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft".

The memo continues: "It's hard to overstate Dan's impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original Xbox in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow – and so much more – we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.".

With Xbox's merger of Playground Games and Turn 10, the developers will be working in collaboration on the Forza and Fable franchises. The final track racer game that Playground Games developed prior to this merger was 2023's Forza Motorsport reboot, a wonderful racer that offered a sweet alternative to the more arcade Forza Horizon series. In Eurogamer's review, the game was described as: "A generous and lavish racer, with thrilling driving, that wants you for the long haul.".

#3837. Godhood was not enough:’ A fan placed tombstones for EA’s most legendary studios at the company’s offices

Electronic Arts’ already-troubled relationship with the gaming community has sunk to new lows in recent weeks, and one anonymous fan turned their anger into something as mournful as it is beautiful: a memorial mural dedicated to the many, many studios EA has killed off over the years.

The mural’s creator unveiled their creation on the r/gaming subreddit. Set up outside EA’s Vancouver headquarters, the piece features seven headstones dedicated to seven major gaming studios EA shut down over the last few decades. Each tombstone lists the year the studio started, the year EA shut it down, and a unique quote inspired by its most well-known games and franchises.

Here’s a more detailed breakdown of the mural, tombstone by tombstone.

In their post, the creator describes the mural as the culmination of their long-simmering frustration with EA, describing the company’s recent decision to shutter Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare as the straw that broke the camel’s back.

“We’ve had EA offices in town for years… decades. But this year, with the timing, I decided that maybe, maybe a little more should be done. So a day of cutting, painting, printing and taping ended with this little display getting set up outside their offices.”

The work has been met with overwhelming positivity. Many praised the mural’s creativity and expressed their own frustration with EA’s tendency to put profit over the people who create its games. Others shared fond memories of the various studios’ work, with franchises like Origin’s Ultima and Westwood’s Command and Conquer getting the lion’s share of attention.

Some observers, however, offered at least some defense of EA, arguing that a few studios on the list (namely BioWare) didn’t always make the best decisions with their most popular properties and that EA’s financial backing gave these studios the chance to make many of their best games.

In an edit responding to these comments, the author acknowledged there was room for nuance in the discussion surrounding EA and its past ventures. That said, they adamantly defend their choice to build the mural, arguing that these studios deserve to be remembered and proudly admitting they would have put the names of other shuttered EA-owned studios like Mythic and Black Box if they’d had more time.

Some games will resonate and land hard. Others just won’t. But running an “up or out” management process inevitably has everyone out.

With EA firmly on track to make more audience-alienating decisions, this is one of many gamers expressing their distaste for the company through art. Anti-EA movements like “Save Mass Effect” already use art to spread their message, so the tombstone-maker is in good company. Maybe there’ll even be some collaboration at some point?

I tried the demo for Queen's Domain last year and liked it a lot⁠—though it definitely had some friction I wasn't sure about. The full game launched on October 30, and I eagerly rushed through the parts I'd already played in the demo.

Turns out, that demo cut out right when things were about to go nuts.

Five hours in out of an estimated 30+, and Queen's Domain is easily one of my top games of the year. I am only begrudgingly writing this, because I'd rather be playing right now.

Queen's Domain starts out resembling other entries in a growing subgenre of indie King's Field-likes, paying homage to the first-person dark fantasy RPG series FromSoftware put out before its soulsward turn. In its first half hour or so, Queen's Domain distinguishes itself similarly to fellow genre standout Lunacid: Fantastic art, maybe even better music, and a mastery of nostalgic intangibles (menu, UI, sound cues, etc.) After beating the first boss, Queen's Domain rewards you with a magic airdash sword, and it's at that point that the game truly begins.

Queen's Domain is a very deliberately paced game and, like a lot of first-person RPGs, it starts out feeling like your boots will always be on the ground. Think the difference between Doom and Quake: You can mostly tell when a game will let you get some air or not.

But once I was rocking the Holy Sword, Endu? Holy shit. Queen's Domain's first area opens up like some wonderful clockwork contraption. A lot of the verticality reminds me of Destiny raids, the way hidden paths blend into the environment, and reaching them feels like you're sequence breaking.

Endu can be upgraded with special gems throughout the game, with each giving you an extra dash while airborne. I'm up to three at the time of writing, and each upgrade has felt like it radically opened up my traversal options: There are parts of the first few maps I'm pretty sure I'll only be able to reach once I'm up to four or five dashes, zooming from one end of the map to the other without touching the ground.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Endu's a standout, but it's not the only tool available: Queen's Domain seems to have an expansive arsenal, and weapons can transform as they're upgraded. You upgrade weapons just by using them, and the game has no stat allocation on level up, encouraging experimentation with the arsenal⁠—PC Gamer hardware writer James Bentley managed to max upgrade 20 weapons across his full playthrough. You can effectively create a "build" via your choice of which weapons to hotkey (limit of three) and upgrade, a system that more resembles BioShock or the System Shock Remake rather than something like Dark Souls or Lunacid.

My favorite alongside Endu so far has been the Caestus, a type of medieval knuckle duster that's been a standby of the Souls games. Here, it's a fast-attacking blunt weapon useful against slashing-resistant skeletons. Instead of a horizontal dash like Endu, its special attack is an uppercut that launches my character into the air. Plenty of fun to use on enemies, but I've loved deploying it as an effective double jump to reach otherwise-inaccessible areas⁠—and there's always been a surprise or meaningful reward waiting for me when I do.

My coworker, PCG staff writer Morgan Park, initially bounced off the pre-Endu, demo-equivalent portion of Queen's Domain. I'm here to say stay strong, prayer warriors. It is worth getting through that first half hour. While there's something to be said about it potentially putting new players off, I think the contrast between pre-and post-Endu gameplay is so strong, it makes the air dash feel all the more powerful. You know what it's like to be stuck on the ground, and you won't take it for granted.

It's the sort of contrast metroidvanias thrive on⁠—I always think of how dinky you feel before you get the wall jump in Hollow Knight⁠—and Queen's Domain's brilliant level design might leave it the best first-person metroidvania anyone's made since the first Metroid Prime.

And I think Prime's a strong comparison point overall here: The cryptic atmosphere, breathtaking vistas, and genuinely unique approach to first-person movement and level design speak to that. I'm already seeing hints toward game-spanning backtracking in my future, but I've got reason to suspect Queen's Domain's backtracking will be less frustrating and obtuse than Metroid Prime's.

I already love this game, and I am about to mainline it over the next 30 hours or so of my free time⁠—stay tuned for our full Queen's Domain review to come. Meanwhile, Queen's Domain is available on Steam for a launch price of $17, down from an MSRP of $20.

#3835. EA reportedly closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between Mass Effect 5 and Star Wars Battlefront 3

And it chose the "less risky, more predictable bet".

A new report has revealed that EA closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between investing in one of two sci-fi projects: a new Mass Effect game or a new Star Wars Battlefront game. And it chose the latter.

The revelation comes from Bloomberg, which heard from "people familiar with the company's strategy" that the "recent emergence" of an opportunity to develop a third Battlefront game meant EA - a company saddled with $18bn in debt because of the recent leveraged buyout - would have two sci-fi projects, each likely to cost hundreds of millions of dollars to make.

It couldn't afford to make both of them so EA executives chose Star Wars Battlefront 3, because it was seen "as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect", Bloomberg reported - despite development for the game not even having begun yet.

An EA spokesperson said the company had "collectively reached this decision following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities". "While this is never easy," the spokesperson went on, "we ultimately have to make tough decisions to focus our teams on the biggest opportunities for our future, including investing in new projects across our portfolio."

The report highlights a few other contributing factors in EA's decision, including BioWare's unfavourable recent track record and a reorganisation of its executive ranks to include more EA Sports people, in favour of those advocating for BioWare. EA bosses even lamented Dragon Age: Veilguard's sales, suggesting it would have been better if the title was 'a live service game'.

Last week, following the announcement of BioWare's closure and the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, an internal video for the project - known as Mass Effect Universe - was leaked, showing what appears to be a pre-rendered visualisation of it. The game was said to take place 600 years after the Reaper war, in the midst of a galactic cold war, and to have the player be "a cross between John Wick and James Bond" in terms of what they'd be capable of.

There was a promise of "Hitman-style freedom" in approaching levels, romance that "wasn't being sanitised", and for connections between the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. It's not clear how much work was done on it, but clearly a lot of planning had been done - far more, certainly, than has been done on Battlefront 3.

EA's Star Wars Battlefront 2 was released in 2017 and struggled, initially, to convince - partly because it was riddled with loot boxes. But years of adjustments and improvements left it in a much better place.

#3834. Fewer genAI clones of "someone else's specific game" should flood the net going forwards, as Anthropic tell Claude to stop messing with some stuff other people own

It will still let people generate "original" games using the tech

Anthropic have told their genAI tool Claude to start ducking requests from users to recreate or clone existing games, following a flood of folks using the tech to generate six-fingered remakes. Instead of risking infringing on the intellectual property of series or titles that companies which aren't Anthropic own, Claude will instead restrict itself to only generating "original" games slopped together based on whatever data it's drawing on.

"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Anthropic staffer Addy Osmani wrote on not Twitter in response to a rando with a cat profile picture having spotted the change.

"Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working," Osmani continued. "We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Game Developer reached out to Anthropic for confirmation and were pointed to Osmani's post.

The change should make it harder to add to the horde of genAI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports which have hit the net recently. It's hardly a surprising one, given studios like Bethesda have seemingly had to take matters into their own lawyers' hands to get the likes of an AI-generated Fallout game taken offline, with games that've just been ripped wholesale or barely tweaked likely on even more perilous ground. That said, not every corp's responded to the DIY decompilation craze by immediately taking legal action.

There's a serious degree of irony to Anthropic slapping Claude and telling it stealing is bad. One of the ways the company develop and train their genAI models is by scraping publicly available data from the internet via a web crawler.

So, some nicking of stuff is bad, little bot people keep asking to regurgitate stuff into slop they can then try to pass off as something they've created. But not all nicking of stuff, lest our whole business be on rather shaky ground.

It's unlikely this move from Anthropic does much to convince actual developers of original games they're safe to put demos of their games out prior to release, without risking dickheads using genAI to clone said demo and potentially release a slop version in rapid fashion, but one can dream of that genie being put back in the bottle someday.

Somehow, Tales of games still hold secrets

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There have been advancements in Tales of technology. 29 years almost to the day after the 1997 Japanese release of Tales of Destiny, the second entry in the still-running Tales of JRPG series, players have found a way to recruit a party member long thought unobtainable.

Shared on YouTube by Kevangelion, who cites help from fellow JRPG scientists SymphoniaLauren, Mziab, and Ethanol, the "Legitimate Lilith Recruit Scene" made waves in this particular JRPG community. Although this was changed in the PS2 re-release of Tales of Destiny, the original PS1 version did not allow you to recruit Lilith Aileros normally. Or so we thought.

It turns out you can recruit Lilith in this version of the game – you just have to jump through more hoops than an aquarium seal working overtime.

The route necessary to recruit Lilith also helps explain why nobody found this until now. If you do anything wrong, you're locked out for good, and the venn diagram of that wrongdoing and normal play is nearly a circle. No typical player would be expected to find or anticipate all of this. This is a caliber of Easter egg that we don't really get anymore – the kind of discovery you only make by digging straight through the stone that you thought to be the bottom of the rabbit hole you've already dug.

In a 26-step guide, Kevangelion summarizes the Japanese forum post surfacing this method. Lilith will join your party in Part 2 of Tales of Destiny if you do everything right – quite forcefully, ironically, with the character exclaiming, "I'm coming with you, like it or not!" – but good luck dodging every possible mistake without a guide.

If you take items from homes, you're out. Dungeon loot is fair game, but even grabbing things like Apple Gel or food from early areas will apparently break the rules. If you manually change protagonist Stahn Aileron's weapon in Part 1, you're out. If you sell or discard the silver ladle weapon, you're out. If you get scolded by NPCs like Rutee Katrea, skip or interrupt certain conversations, annoy some merchants, or talk to Lilith more than once in Leene's Village, the whole route seemingly falls apart.

Kevangelion's summary sounds simple: "The route assumes: a 'clean,' obedient Stahn who listens and does not pick fights with the plot — no house loot, follow destination prompts, keep conversations moving." But as soon as you dig into the specifics, you find a mine field of ways to accidentally push Lilith out of the picture.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"The fact that this was discovered almost three decades after this game's initial release is crazy work, it makes me wonder what other secrets in other Tales games have not yet been discovered," one user speculates in a YouTube comment. At this point in the longest release gap in series history, I'll take anything Tales-shaped to tide me over.

Plenty of users still happy to deposit their funds into the cryptocurrency exchange nevertheless.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Binance saw a huge outpouring of withdrawals when it re-opened to customers on Sunday following a hack for the history books. The cryptocurrency exchange lost $6.3 billion, roughly $3 billion of which was frozen in transit and the rest covered by the company, but it lost a bunch more once it let customers take their money out on November 1.

Customers withdrew $4.649 billion from the exchange in just under 10 hours since it reopened. That's a whole lot of value to lose in a day, and not wholly surprising given the context, but what is more surprising is how many deposits were made in that same timeframe: roughly $1 billion worth.

"Withdrawals were temporarily suspended as a precaution while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services, and complete security checks," Binance said of the move.

Users may face slowdowns as systems get back up and running, the company has said.

In later updates, Binance says that deposits into the exchange have begun to creep back up in excess of withdrawals; the total cashflow of the crypto exchange is still a net negative, at -$5 billion by November 3, but the withdrawals are no longer outpacing the deposits by any significant amount. It's still early days and a long way to go to make up for the initial loss in customer funds, but the exchange may still live to fight another day.

Withdrawal data update By 03:00 UTC, we are seeing hourly deposits exceed withdrawals, reflecting improving user activity and stabilizing flows. https://t.co/UiXmYC2lm3November 3, 2026

Meanwhile, the exact details of the attack are still being deliberated. The FBI holds North Korea responsible, agreeing with experts that a group going by the name of TraderTraitor is behind it. The FBI says that it, along with USSS and IRS-CI, has observed the group converting the stolen crypto into Ether, with a view to launder it away into obscurity later.

North Korea, unsurprisingly, denies the FBI's claim. Kim Yo Jong, an official in the NK government, and Kim Jong Un's sister, said it was nothing more than a "sinister attempt" by the US to damage the country's reputation.

Crimson Desert is one of 2026's most successful releases. The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

"When you're on the eve of releasing a game that keeps you all employed, work's more important"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wardogs CEO Joe Brammer has defended the long hours his team had to put into the early access release of its FPS hit, declaring the anti-crunch attitude of some other developers as "Californian bullshit."

Speaking to Edge, Brammer explains the some of his philosophy behind the high standards of recruitment Wardogs studio Bulkhead has adopted. In the past, Brammer has said that the Wardgos team checks the Steam accounts of applicants to see if they're genuinely passionate about FPS games. "We liked how talent-driven the industry used to be," Brammer says. "And then it started to be about 'everybody should be able to get a job in games.' We don't really think like that."

Brammer thinks "the floodgates opened" for games industry hiring, "but now they're closing again, and there might be some benefit to saying to people: 'you have to be fucking good to be here, and you have to prove your worth.'"

Some of that involves working late hours, but Brammer argues that's sometimes a necessary evil. "Our team doesn't love working late, but they do work late and we do crunch. What we're saying is that sometimes, yes, life is more important. But sometimes, when you're on the eve of releasing a game that keeps you all employed, work's more important."

Brammer's philosophy stems from his own family. "My mum was a teacher and a headteacher at a school," he says. "I've never seen someone do so much crunch for barely any money. And so when game devs are like 'I don't want to work overtime for my 100K salary'? Fuck. Off. Respectfully, it's Californian bullshit."

Known for being pretty direct in his communication, Brammer has also told his players not to expect much from the team over the coming weeks. Ahead of a month-long break in December to celebrate Wardog's early access success, he told fans to "go play GTA 6" because "we need to detox" and said that he wants "to make sure players know they can fuck off" for a month while Bulkhead takes a break.

Wardogs is getting loadouts, CEO confirms, but the devs want you to "keep trying different weapons rather than settling on one setup."

#3826. How to find and defeat A$AP Rocky boss in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

While plundering for bounty across the vast Treasure Hunters island in Fortnite, you’ll oftentimes encounter unique characters hanging around. One such individual is A$AP Rocky, a special boss you can track down and defeat in battle.

Bosses are great foes to eliminate when you’re on the hunt for some special loot, and taking them out is also commonly part of key quests. If you’re having trouble pinpointing this one, here’s how to find and defeat the A$AP Rocky boss in Fortnite.

You can find the A$AP Rocky boss hanging out at The $$ Rocky in Fortnite. This location is a main, named POI situated near the middle right edge of the island. A$AP Rocky can be found wandering around the top end of the island, slightly north of the large grey boat that’s docked at this POI.

While most other recent seasons have had bosses spawn randomly around lots of different spots, A$AP Rocky functions differently and is a lot easier to find. He only ever appears at this spot, so as long as another player hasn’t beaten you to fighting him, you’ll always find him here.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

A$AP Rocky is pretty similar to most other bosses that have appeared in Fortnite, which means his combat style is generally pretty clunky, and his aim is fairly bad. He does, however, use a rocket launcher to fight you, which means if his shots do strike you, they take a good chunk of your health away.

He also jumps around quite a bit and moves a lot more swiftly than most other opponents. This is thanks to the special shock rock chargers his unique weapon supplies during combat.

To successfully defeat A$AP Rocky in combat, focus on maintaining your distance and being prepared to dodge whenever he fires a rocket your way. Watch his movements and behavior so you know when the rocket launcher is loaded, as it’s imperative you don’t let any of his shots strike you.

You don’t need much to take him out, but it’s a good idea to have at least two weapons and a decent amount of ammo before taking on A$AP Rocky. Then, all you need to do is keep firing until his health bar is depleted.

Upon being defeated in battle, A$AP Rocky drops the Exotic A$AP Rocky’s Shock Rocket weapon. This is a powerful, high-impact rocket launcher that can be used to fire deadly explosives at opponents. Defeating A$AP Rocky is the only way to get your hands on it.

This weapon has the special ability to grant you shock charges while you wield it. These charges can be consumed for a helpful boost while jumping, making traversal around the island much easier overall.

Additionally, he always drops the Lil’ Flacko Sprite for you to add to your collection. You also need some ammo to get started using the Exotic A$AP Rocky’s Shock Rocket item, so he grants you some rockets.

If you’re looking for more to do after you’re done taking on A$AP Rocky in battle, there’s plenty to choose from. Next, you might consider collecting map fragments, using Sprite Wanted Posters to dig up and open Sprite Chests, and unlocking Solid Gold A$AP Rocky.

#3825. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

Final Fantasy 14's queues can get long—not for roulettes, mind, those are usually pretty nippy—but if you're trying to complete a specific alliance raid as a newer player, you can be stuck twiddling your thumbs for ages.

Square Enix is planning to make a change that'll fix that soon, though. In a recent blog post to the game's website, it's been announced that same-region player matchmaking'll be available starting November 10 after a successful trial period on its Japanese servers.

What does that mean? Basically, FF14's server architecture is into physical data centers (Japan, Europe, Oceania, and North America), then logical data centers, which are sort of like realms in other MMOs. For instance, the NA servers have Crystal, Aether, Dynamis, and Primal (then within those centers are "worlds", which can be travelled and matchmade between pretty easily).

You've been able to hop between these logical data centers manually for some time—it's pretty common, for instance, for Crystal players to hop on over to Aether to group up with folks for high-end content. But you need to log out to do so, with said parties constructed through the in-game party finder.

After November 10, however, matchmaking for things like roulettes will also be possible within the same physical data center, as will the party finder writ large, cross-world linkshells, fellowships, and friend list and /tell functionality. Travelling between data centers will also be made easier, too.

This is a huge quality-of-life boost that should massively cut down on queueing times—but it'll also make organising or creating groups for the aforementioned high-end content way easier, too, allowing folks to see and join listings for different logical data centers without having to hop between them.

My secret hope, as an EU player who's currently stuck on North American ping for community reasons (it's where all my mates are), is that this sort of functionality might one day lead to cross region travel so I can hop on over to the EU whenever I actually want to do content. A guy can dream.

#3823. Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3's online servers are temporarily going dark, FromSoftware announces

Things might get even darker over in the world of Lordran without those silly, only sometimes helpful notes left by other players. Developer FromSoftware has announced that it's temporarily closing Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 servers because of an unspecified issue.

"Due to a server issue, the game servers for the following titles will be temporarily unavailable on all platforms," the RPG studio tweeted earlier today, before naming Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3.

While the server shutdown won't last forever, FromSoftware hasn't told series fans when exactly they can expect online play to be restored. That presumably means PvP invasions, summon signs and in-game messages that try to troll you off a cliff are unavailable for the time being.

"We will provide updates once we have information regarding the server restoration time. We apologize for the inconvenience," the studio added. I hope you've stocked up on Estus Flasks, at least.

Of course, this isn't the first time the Dark Souls trilogy has had to contend with server problems. In 2022, Bandai Namco took servers for all three Dark Souls games offline due to a security vulnerability affecting Dark Souls 3. The threequel went dark once again a few months later.

FromSoftware's next game The Duskbloods - the one with the jetpacks and vampires and a cute bird thing - hasn't been any luckier, either. The multiplayer-focused game's first network test had to be taken offline early due to similarly vague "server issues". More recently, FromSoftware delayed its Switch 2 exclusive into next year.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," the developer tweeted this week. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

#3822. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

#3821. How to contact Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

Weekly quests often challenge you to tackle fairly specific, strange tasks you’re not likely to attempt otherwise in Fortnite. One such mission asks you to contact Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port.

Any mission that asks you to track down a specific item around the vast island is tough, as there are loads of unique locations to explore, and you’re looking for one very small item hidden around them. It’s a tough task to get done, so here’s how to contact Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port in Fortnite.

You can find the Slone Phone in a brick building near the northeast end of the Plunder Port POI. This location is situated near the very southern end of the island. To find the Slone Phone, visit this spot and head over to the north end of the area, where there are a few different buildings you can explore, rather than the port, which has two ships docked at it.

At Plunder Port, look for the large, two-story brick warehouse building. It’s fairly close to the bright pink flamingo ship docked near the east end of this location. This building also has a large slurp tank slightly sticking out of it, so you can look for this to help you find the right spot.

Inside this building, walk around to the back of the large silver slurp tank. Turn right to find a small storage room. On the ground in front of the wooden shelves, you’ll find the Slone Phone.

Once you’re somewhat close to the right building, a white diamond icon with an exclamation point will appear, marking the precise location of the Slone Phone. You do have to be fairly close to it for this symbol to pop up, though, so finding the general region for it first is essential.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

To complete the contact Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port quest, you need to find and answer the Slone Phone at Plunder Port. The tough part of this mission is tracking down the small phone, but once you’ve found it, all you need to do is hold down the button that pops up next to the “Answer” text when looking at it. As soon as you do, this mission will be complete.

There are lots of other tricky missions you may want to tackle after checking off this one. Next, consider working on collecting a map fragment at The $.$. Rocky, using Sprite Wanted Posters to dig up and open Sprite Chests, and unlocking Solid Gold A$AP Rocky.

Nintendo and Blizzard aren't competing with Rockstar in the same way as some

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All the games that have rushed their release dates out of November in response to Grand Theft Auto 6's November 19 launch have indirectly handed other big hitters like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (out November 8) and World of Warcraft: Forever (out November 4) a remarkably open month. It can seem like Rockstar's done Nintendo and Blizzard a favor here, especially when these three games don't compete on the same platforms, but there's more to this month.

Ahead of the GTA 6 launch, I spoke to analyst Mat Piscatella, games lead at Circana. He's unsurprisingly confident that GTA 6, as the leader of the holiday rush, will help drive increased spending in the industry and, hopefully, bring in more players who will attract more investment which eventually leads to more good games. In this rush, he sizes up the November fear that's seen so many studios push up or delay their launches to avoid sitting next to Rockstar.

"I'm sure it's a little different for everyone who decided to move their game out, whether it was a feeling of direct competition or just not wanting to try to grab any air and have it all be suffocated away by Grand Theft Auto," Piscatella reasons. "I don't know, that's all an individual developer or publisher decision. But if I have a cozy sim or a first-person shooter or, I don't know, a puzzle platformer walking sim, I don't know why I would necessarily move my game for Grand Theft Auto. But hey, people are probably just scared of potentially running into this game. So we'll see.

"World of Warcraft: Forever is also coming out, and that's on PC where Grand Theft Auto isn't, so I'm sure those games are going to be just fine. The Switch 2 audience that isn't invested in PlayStation or Xbox at all, of course they're going to be very interested in Zelda, and even some Grand Theft Auto players are very interested in Zelda. We have about, according to our latest tracking, 15% of people who intend to buy Grand Theft Auto also intend to buy [the Ocarina of Time remake]. We have a lot of crossover there too. The thing's been built up so big, and absolutely warranted, but everyone just kind of moved and perhaps they didn't need to."

The interesting thing is that, despite enormous differences in tone, look, gameplay, audience, platform, and just about everything else, GTA 6 and the Ocarina of Time remake do have a fair bit in common when you zoom out. Piscatella notes that they both "lean more towards the more mature portions of the market in terms of age ranges," tap into nostalgia to varying degrees, and will lean toward "affluent folks" who can stomach today's console prices. How terrifying it is for GTA 5 to be so old that it can reasonably be called nostalgic.

"All that stuff's coming together to make it a great environment for this game to launch right now. Well, great given everything happening with pricing and supply constraints and the RAM crisis and everything else," Piscatella observes.

But has Rockstar actually helped Blizzard or Nintendo indirectly? "Maybe," Piscatella says. But "with Nintendo first-party games on Nintendo platforms, it's always an open window because that's primarily what those platforms are used for by folks." A new Zelda remaking one of the best-known games of all time was always going to hit hard. It just works out nicely that GTA 6 can top PS5 and Xbox Series X, Ocarina is the big Switch 2 title for November, and WoW: Forever could hardly ask for less competition on PC.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

You can understandably argue that there's never really an open window given the volume of games coming out every year, the number of free-to-play games available, and the amount of time and money being poured into the same live services. All games face competition at all times. But games will dodge each other for a reason, and looking at core platforms and premium new releases, the stars have really aligned this November.

Piscatella notes that WoW: Forever is also a nostalgia play. "There's probably going to be some crossover there," he says. "It's come on real hot with the beta – wasn't really thinking about it before that beta, but the beta was so strong in terms of reaction and participation. It's a little bit of a dark horse in terms of its overall impact, but it could be something. It also has a pretty open-ish window, even though there's no open windows on PC anymore because of everything going on.

"But these three games? Great. Everything else in the market, we'll see. We'll see what happens for everything else that's come out in September and October, and everything that's going to be coming out in January, February that got pushed out. We'll see what the blast radius really is on this thing."

#3819. Blizzard hints at console ports for World of Warcraft: Forever - "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want"

After more than two decades dominating the PC MMO battlefield, it sounds like Blizzard Entertainment's taking the idea of a World of Warcraft console port more seriously than ever.

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta seems to have been immensely popular with fans of the series. It's a brand new third version of the iconic multiplayer game that sits alongside WoW's Classic and Retail portions, and it's recaptured many a lapsed Warcraft sicko with tons of good changes, big and small - one of which is controller support for the first time ever.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the decision to keep World of Warcraft: Forever exclusive to PC players, despite now supporting gamepads, vice president and executive producer Holly Longdale hinted that the fantasy game might just make its way to even more devices and players over time.

"What you just described is really what we're after," she told the outlet. "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want. But the first leg of that journey is getting gamepads working really well with World of Warcraft, and we thought Forever was the perfect place to start."

Longdale reckons all gaming platforms might become "more ubiquitous" in the future, as well. She specifically named the Xbox Project Helix, which is said to be a PC-console hybrid device of some kind. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed the next-gen console can even play your PC games earlier in the year.

"Honestly, we just want to be able to play it anywhere. We've seen people getting it working on the ROG Ally X," Longdale added. "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

World of Warcraft: Forever properly launches on the 4th of November.

Despite struggles in the rest of the Xbox division, Forever's beta was supposedly the "largest" in series history. Elsewhere, Longdale acknowledged that some of the developer's decisions won't make everybody equally happy: "I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"

#3818. "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight

"I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it"

Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

Overwatch's skin distribution is, in one word, lopsided. With a roster of 54 heroes and counting it can be hard to ensure that every character gets their fair share of cosmetics as is, but when you add popularity into the mix it gets even harder.

As a free-to-play game, Overwatch makes the bulk of its money through cosmetics like bundles or standalone skins. Skins also take a good amount of time to prototype and create, so to ensure its efforts aren't wasted the team needs to pick heroes based on how many players will actually buy the end product.

"Every new piece of content that we introduce to the game, whether it's a hero or even a map, you know, means that the pool of everything that we've got, it is spread out a little bit," game director Aaron Keller says in a group interview (via Kotaku). This leaves room for two kinds of heroes to get regular skins. There's popular heroes like Ana, Genji, and Soldier 76 which are played by a large proportion of players and then there's the fan favourites who aren't just popular but have a dedicated playerbase who will consistently buy skins like Mercy, Kiriko, Juno, and Widowmaker.

However, Team 4 has, in recent years, made a clear effort to bulk up cosmetics for new heroes. "Constantly expanding our capacity" to create skins for characters like Anran, Freyja, and Vendetta who have all been included in recent skin collabs. And while the devs have been able to create more skins than those that just "support the actual bottom-line business", money still needs to be made.

It's kind of like a pay-it-forward system. By making cosmetics that will sell well, Team 4 are able to dedicate time and energy to heroes that won't yield as much of a monetary gain. "The place that you can see that most transparently is the Mythic skins that we release," Keller adds. "Each season we release two Mythic skins, and typically one of those is going to be for a hero that we think is actually going to really drive a lot of that support for the business. And then another one is going to be for a hero that typically hasn't gotten either a Mythic or a lot of other skins in the recent past."

I recognise that I'm probably in a fortunate position where my main, Ana, has always had a healthy amount of new and very cool cosmetics. But the point still stands that this is a business, so Team 4 needs to make responsible financial decisions for reasons that are at times out of their control.

"We recognize it's important to players," Keller says. "We want to be doing as much of it as we can, but we still always want to be doing it in a way that's also responsible, and [lets us] know that we can continue supporting this game going forward."

The devs themselves turned their "almost androgynous" hero into the Lara Croft we know, but the marketing "showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lara Croft was once gaming's biggest sex symbol, but it wasn't always meant to be that way. The original Tomb Raider devs first envisioned their hero as a more realistic and androgynous woman before settling on the Lara we'd eventually know. But even though the devs at Core Design turned Lara Croft into a polygonal hourglass, they still weren't thrilled to see publisher Eidos lean into a sex-first marketing strategy.

"Lara was originally Latina and her appearance was more realistic, almost androgynous," co-creator and lead programmer Paul Douglas tells The Guardian. "We felt that more stylised movement would play better, so her physique changed to reflect that." Lara's origins as a Latin American character called Laura Cruz are well documented, but much of the Cruz concept art that's surfaced over the years still depicts her with exaggerated hips and a bare midriff.

The common wisdom among publishers at the time was that "a female character will never sell," as Douglas puts it. But even if Eidos initially saw Lara as a marketing liability, that quickly changed. She was put front and center in the marketing for the first Tomb Raider game, and by the time the sequels came around, Eidos was happily releasing pin-up style renders of the character in increasingly suggestive stages of undress.

"The marketability of Lara thrust Tomb Raider into the stratosphere," Douglas says. "The game’s publisher, Eidos Interactive, took the character and ran with it. I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of the way Lara was sexualised."

Level designer Heather Stevens agrees. "Eidos saw the potential of Lara, rather than the game, so they focused on her," she remarks. "That was the right thing to do, but I think it went a bit too far with what she was wearing or the poses she was put in for some marketing campaigns. They showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her."

Ironically, it wouldn't be until the 2013 Tomb Raider reboot from Crystal Dynamics that Lara would be rendered in a way approaching the original, "realistic" vision – though calling the modern Lara "androgynous" would certainly be a stretch. Either way, the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst and Legacy of Atlantis are once again leaning into a more campy, exaggerated vision of Lara Croft. I suspect we won't see as many boudoir-style pin-ups of her this time around, however.

These are the best Tomb Raider games of all time.

#3813. Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.

In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?

Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.
