I only get the urge to play Minecraft every six months or so now, but those few weeks are always full of the best times—whether that be working on my expanding underground dwarven city or in my friend's Skyblock server where I'm forced to farm dirt.

Rory Norris: While Minecraft is already a very competent, incredibly cosy sandbox—my only ask is furniture in a game about building things—it's a totally different beast with mods. Eclipsing Skyrim, I'd say Minecraft is the most modded, transformable game ever. You can add furniture because Mojang oddly refuses too (I'm not mad), turn it into a Souls-inspired RPG, or make it a factory automation game. It's timeless. Like Skyrim, I'll always get the annual urge to return to it.

Harvey Randall: I somehow always become the guy who goes and mines stuff in my multiplayer servers. This probably says something about the nature of my soul.

Shaun Prescott: Creative mode is one of the best cosy, meditative experiences on PC.

Released: February 24, 2022 | Top 100 Score: 254.90

Sean Martin: What if Dark Souls embraced the open world formula? It's a simple concept, but Elden Ring stands testament to how successfully it was realised. Take FromSoft's iconic combat, boss fights, and quests, then explode them into an enigmatic world you slowly explore and unravel. I have over 800 hours in Elden Ring (plus 500 in Nightreign) and I still started a new playthrough when Tarnished Edition released.

Andy Chalk: I don't like Souls games but I loved Elden Ring, because it let me avoid the whole Souls thing: Instead of all that dodge-parry-slash nonsense (and no offense if that's what you're into, but brother, I am not), I just gave myself a big brain with a big stick, and melted everything. Some fans of the genre might say I deprived myself of the 'real' Souls experience, but I got to enjoy one of the most stunning fantasy worlds I've ever explored—something I'd have missed if the game hadn't been willing to let me play it on my own terms.

Harvey Randall: I have played Elden Ring (and its expansion) exactly once, and I will admit, I've not had the stomach to do so a second time—the scope of these games is a touch overwhelming to me. But that one playthrough did utterly enthral and capture me, so I can't complain too much. Besides, Sean plays enough Elden Ring for all of us.

Issy van der Velde: Elden Ring is the antithesis of the focus found in Sekiro, and it still rules. I love that Andy could have fun melting everyone while I got to enjoy shredding them with a big spikey wheel axe.

Released: May 18, 2015 | Top 100 Score: 258.38

Ted Litchfield: I was late to the party (maybe not so much in the grand scheme) getting The Witcher 3 for Christmas in 2015. Velen is great, but things really clicked for me in Novigrad. One of my fondest gaming memories remains sitting on a beanbag in my parents' basement over the break, my chunky, already-aging laptop plugged into the TV with its fans screaming. I was rocking a first gen, owl-faced Steam Controller, and I was so invested in the search for Sigi Reuven's treasure that I pulled an all-nighter by accident.

11 years on, The Witcher 3 is still, somehow, one of the best-looking videogames out there, its balance of art direction and photorealism gracefully aging like a DILF-y Hollywood leading man. I think CDPR has managed to at least match the achievement of The Witcher 3 with Cyberpunk, but that's hardly a universal opinion, and Geralt's final(?) outing remains a triumph.

Jody Macregor: I do think The Witcher 3 has a magic Cyberpunk 2077 didn't match. The way it's structured incentivises pushing on in your search for Yennefer and then Ciri without feeling like you have such limited time you can't engage with whichever of its many excellent sidequests catches your interest. There's just enough impetus to keep up the momentum without making you feel like it's out-of-character to have a little fun. And if you crank the difficulty up Geralt's combat style (prep-heavy research-based battle herbalism) is actually great.

Andy Chalk: One of my favorite things about The Witcher 3 (and spoiler here, but it's been a decade) is that when all is said and done—if you played your cards reasonably right—Geralt gets a happy ending. I like happy endings, and if any videogame guy deserves one, it's Geralt. That dude powered through some shit, and as much as I'd like his adventures to continue, the send-off CD Projekt gave him with Blood and Wine left me far happier to call it done.

Joshua Wolens: Geralt of Rivia will return in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past, and so help me CDPR if you do anything bad to him I'm picketing your offices.

Andy Chalk: Yeah, just a little follow-up to my previous comment here: If CD Projekt does a Vesemir to Geralt, I am gonna be setting shit on fire.

Released: October 15, 2019 | Top 100 Score: 259.74

Ted Litchfield: Disco Elysium was the game that made me get serious about a career in games. It's now one of the biggest bummers I have to deal with professionally. The IP ownership and financial allegations? Byzantine. The interpersonal strife among its developers? Distressing. The layoffs and lives upended in its wake? To quote my man Geralt of Rivia, Poland's most soulful white boy from the previous entry on this list: It's "the last bitter drop in a chalice of sorrow."

And yet. Cut to the game underneath it all, and you'll still find a potentially life-changing work of baffling, miraculous provenance. Punks don't know how to make each other do the dishes without a struggle session. How the fuck did they make a game?

Six years on, it's easy to take Disco's design innovations for granted: Strip the so-so combat out of Planescape: Torment and replace it with a union of RPG and point 'n click adventure. Dialogue windows in the bottom-center of the screen with walls of text suck, so hammer it into a much more parsable, right-oriented vertical feed instead. Have the skills you invest in not only open opportunities, but shift the tone of the experience with their distinctive, hallucinatory personalities.

Disco tells a story with heart and characters that feel real, set in a tiny slice of a world that blends alternate history with pure fantasy like the best 20th century sci-fi writers, your Le Guins, Herberts, and Dicks. Its authors were people of strong social and political conviction who nevertheless trusted players enough to let them disagree and take the story in wildly different directions without it feeling like a failure state.

As I grow older, I've become more partial to stories that end. But we didn't get our fill of Elysium, and I still hope we can go back, someday.

Fraser Brown: A lot of the writing around Disco focuses on how weird it is, or how wonderful it is to have a videogame that's actually funny, and all of those things are true. But what really sticks with me is how heartbreaking it is. It's one of the only videogames to ever make my eyes get a bit leaky. Underneath all the high concept weirdness and political orienteering, it's an incredibly human game that hits like a fucking truck. We'll never see its like again.

Phil Savage: Heartbreaking, yes, but also hopeful. That's the thing that I wasn't expecting when I finally played it earlier this year. Not hopeful in an "everything's going to be OK" kind of way, Disco's optimism is both smaller and grander than that. Everything is not going to be OK, and maybe that's OK. Maybe, if you work on yourself, you can find some meaning in that. Maybe the arthropods are in silent and meaningless awe of you.

Harvey Randall: While you're distracted thinking about everything said above, I'm going to take this chance to go on record and say that I want to marry Kim Kitsuragi. That is all.

Issy van der Velde: I went into Disco Elysium with high expectations, but what I didn't anticipate was the mirror it would hold up to me. It made me realise I'll always be an addict at heart, but it also reaffirmed my desire to overcome that. I didn't let Harry relapse even though he's only pixels and words. I'm flesh and bone, so surely I deserve even better?

Released: August 3, 2023 | Top 100 Score: 270.30

Fraser Brown: Here we are again. Baldur's Gate 3 is our number one game for another year, and let's face it—it's probably going to be taking this spot again in 2027. It's just so damn impressive. There are few games I can say this about, but if you don't get on with BG3, I don't think we can be friends (just don't tell my partner, who doesn't remotely understand the hype). This is one of the best ever RPG studios firing on all cylinders, building on decades of experience and experiments. I hope RPGs haven't peaked with BG3, but I'm struggling to imagine a future where this doesn't continue to be my favourite game of all time.

Sean Martin: I don't even like Dungeons & Dragons that much, and yet I'm one of only 3% of players who've completed the game in Honour Mode. I'm not even sure how that happened? Baldur's Gate 3 is just so damn enchanting. The prospect of adventure, the wonderfully written characters, and the endless twists and turns your journey takes amount to a truly unique gaming experience. I still consider myself blessed that I got to see the orchestral concert in London where Andrew Wincott appeared and sang Raphael's Final Act, because that song is an all-timer.

Jody Macgregor: The Forgotten Realms isn't always an interesting backdrop for roleplaying, and I say that as someone who has run multiple campaigns there. Larian turned it into one by making the obligatory Realms stuff a delight—Volo the travelling disaster, Elminster the cheese freak—and pulling in cool bits from other D&D settings like githyanki and illithids so the world feels slightly alien and part of a larger cosmology. BG3 is a fantasy RPG through and through, but one that restores some of the genre's sense of wonder.

The thing that really makes it special is the reactivity. Act 3 is constantly referencing stuff you did in Act 1, and I only just found out if you take over the newspaper you can print your own stories, changing the city folk's ambient dialogue. Everything you do feels like it matters.

Ted Litchfield: 2023, '24, and much of '25 were dominated by BG3 for me, and it's been a second since I fired it up. I've been on a real Owlcat kick (we'll get Wrath of the Righteous or Rogue Trader on this list next year, prayer warriors), and when my favorite game is no longer right in front of me, my feckless heart can drift. Was it really that good?

Yes. Unequivocally. Universal heavyweight champion of the world. Just thinking about it for this write up has me wanting to roll a new guy⁠—I've never uninstalled, and I don't think I ever will barring force majeure. Larian simultaneously raised the bar on cinematic RPG storytelling while matching the crunchiest classics in depth and complexity. Common sense previously dictated that the two were mutually exclusive, and it feels like CRPGs can finally look forward, not back.

Harvey Randall: I have about 380 hours in this thing. I've completed it twice, once on honour mode, and I got another two extra honour mode playthroughs to Act 3 before I got distracted and left them in the dirt.

I can confidently call it one of the best RPGs that will perhaps ever be made. There's something about the sheer scope of it, the mixture of immersive sim style branching narratives and CRPG goodness that mashes up with professional, glossy production value and fully motion-captured cutscenes.

And while the TTRPG rules lover in me balks at Larian's irreverently-designed magic items which, let's be clear, grab D&D 5e's intended balance and snap it mercilessly over its knee… I'm still very glad they're there. They make the game a min-maxxer's delight.

Currently, I've been roped into an Honor Mode playthrough with Josh, Sean, and Ted, and my Cleric has stumbled onto a build that debuffs everybody just by standing around her. They can attest that I have made some utterly disgusting laugh-noises whenever I knock someone prone with Reverberation just for looking at me funny.

Surprise! There are more than 100 good videogames. Below you'll find a selection of individual recommendations—each a game that a member of the PC Gamer team thinks you should play.

Tyler Wilde, US Editor-in-Chief: Rocket League hasn't evolved much since 2015, but that's because it was already a perfectly-designed competitive team game which no one has yet improved upon. Playing soccer with rocket-powered cars has a high skill ceiling, but great teamwork can trump individual skill, which has led to some of the most exciting underdog wins of my gaming career. I'll be playing when I'm 80 if they don't turn the servers off before then.

John Strike, Senior Art Editor: Big pies. Flat beer. Crazy northeners. Drunk cows. Thank Goodness You’re Here! has it all and then some. This beautiful cartoon-style slapstick romp around the fictional and truly bizarre Yorkshire town of Barnsworth is a must-play for anyone with a soft spot for northern ways. Put your trousers on, grab your net and go and catch those spirit level bubbles!

Elie Gould, News Writer: Oh my god, I forgot to put Silent Hill f on the voting list. This is unforgivable considering how amazing it is and how well it managed to pave the way for the new kind of Silent Hill we're now seeing unfold. Its setting is chilling, mysterious, and cool as all hell, it gives us the best female protagonist I've seen in years, and we're tested with some seriously tricky puzzles and grotesque monsters. It's the whole package.

Christopher Livingston, Senior Editor: After a long absence I finally returned to Rare's open world ocean sandbox this year, and yep, there's still really no other game like it. The beauty of its world and water is still unmatched and there's nowhere else I've found that shares its blend of chill hangout vibes (90%) and humbling PvP nightmare (10%). All you can bring into each session are your skills because there's nothing else to give any pirate an advantage over another. One of a kind.

Rory Norris, Guides Writer: TESO is my most played game of all time, sitting at well over 2,000 hours in the decade since launch. It's an Elder Scrolls game but multiplayer, and it's been carrying the torch while the mainline series has been radio silent since Skyrim. You can explore almost all of Tamriel at this point, questing, doing world bosses, dungeons, and whatnot. And while it's technically a bit of a mess, the large-scale PvP is truly a sight to behold.

Ted Litchfield, Associate Editor: This one was supposed to be on the list proper, sorry everyone. Deadlock, I love you sweetie, but you're not finished. Step aside for what will be PCG's 2025 RPG of the year barring a coup and my execution. Esoteric Ebb riffs on Disco Elysium, but meaningfully pushes the evolving subgenre forward with smart changes like 6 attributes instead of 24 skills, potentially even greater reactivity⁠—especially in its handwritten turn-based battles⁠—and a comedic, hopeful, tone to set its excellent story apart.

Jody Macgregor, Weekend Editor: I may be a turn-based lover who sometimes thinks we should add Jagged Alliance to the Top 100, but even I know there have been a couple of classic RTSes, chief among them Dawn of War. It's got the best sense of scale of any game in the genre, a real feeling of ants versus bison as you build up to tanks and daemons, and the Definitive Edition lets you pull the camera back to appreciate it. Good luck, ants.

Joshua Wolens, News Writer: A 2024 narrative adventure that's more or less a visual novel, 1000xResist is one of those games that make you realise how narratively unambitious most other videogames are. It's about killing god, doing a revolution, inheriting trauma, inflicting trauma, the immigrant experience, the Hong Kong protests, original sin, noodles, and a lot else. It's like a modern Planescape: Torment, in that it's so tenderly and confidently written that it just makes all the other guys look bad.

Evan Lahti, Strategic Director: If you're an XCOM person with any affection for '80s/'90s action movies, JA3 should be your next game. It's campy, it's tropical, and your mercenaries (through story or tactical decisions) can find themselves in no-win scenarios. But my favorite detail is the simmy ballistics: bullets aren't just particle effects, they're physical objects that can scatter randomly and catch collateral hits against enemies, friendlies, civs, or scenery. The campaign itself is delightfully tabletop in its combo of scripted stuff and freedom.

Issy van der Velde, Deputy Editor, PC Gaming Show: Transistor has the best sci-fi love story I've ever experienced, and the combat is endlessly satisfying. Each ability can be used on its own, added to another to create a secondary effect, or held as a passive buff. It's easy to see how Supergiant built on this to create the boons in Hades. Everyone should play this masterpiece for Ashley Barrett and Darren Korb's soundtrack alone. There's even a dedicated button that lets you hum along to the music.

Phil Savage, Global Editor-in-Chief: If you like the idea of Blue Prince, but don't like the roguelike elements, then I have two things to tell you: 1) You are weak and need to fix yourself, and 2) you should play Lorelei and the Laser Eyes. Simogo's mystery box adventure is an absolute treat of puzzle design, cleverly laying out its challenges in cascading threads of discovery. It's deeply satisfying to solve both the individual puzzles and the building mystery of its story. A genuine treat.

Andy Chalk, US News Lead: The Plants vs. Zombies remaster that dropped in 2025 took some heat for technical shortcomings and allegations of AI art, but EA's addressed most of the complaints and these days it stands as a really good remaster of an all-time classic. The original is still available too, and much cheaper, and it holds up remarkably well for its age. Either way, Plants vs. Zombies is a short, snappy, incredibly cute and easy-to-engage tower defense game that remains as great—and essential—as ever.

Sean Martin, Senior Guides Writer: I'm unsure why my compatriots turned on Total War this year, but I'm here to remind you that Three Kingdoms is still incredible. Its quality is often overshadowed by its early demise, but it's quite unlike anything Creative Assembly ever made, or will likely make again. It channels the courageous characters, political machinations, and endless scheming of China's most culturally iconic period into a top-tier strategy game, achieving a harmonious balance between history and romance.

Andrea Shearon, Evergreen Writer: I've been enjoying the survival crafting renaissance, and by that I mean playing the hell out of Abiotic Factor and Enshrouded. The unbelievably detailed, massive high-fantasy RPG has one of the best building systems I've ever seen, and I love rescuing new villagers and crafters to slowly grow my own town. My only complaint is that Embervale is so pretty that I spend dozens of hours whispering, "Oh, maybe I'll settle down here," without getting anything done.

Morgan Park, Staff Writer: A gritty, unforgiving rally racing sim set in outer space. Exo Rally takes an already challenging rally format and adds gravity and thrusters into the mix. You'll tear your hair out trying to complete a singular turn on the moon, then ride the high of circumventing most of a track through well-timed thruster use. I haven't played enough yet to make my case for on the list, but it's turning me into a racing fan. A brilliant 2026 indie that's flying too low under the radar.

Mollie Taylor, Features Producer: I'm 13 years late to the party, but Project Zomboid's brutal, complex, and ridiculously moreish take on zombie survival has gripped me this year. It's one of the most customisable sandbox games I've ever tinkered with, meaning you can go for an unforgiving post-apocalyptic landscape or fine-tune it into a cosy (if not slightly gritty and terrifying) zombified The Sims 1. One of the few games I've been happy to sink hundreds of hours into learning.

Jacob Ridley, Managing Editor, Hardware: There are some games you can sink hour after hour into and not even realise it's already morning. Valheim is one of those games. Jump in with a couple of friends and build a new homestead, trying to one-up each other with ever more elaborate creations (our Sistine Chapel are two rival towers on top of massive rocks). Or just go exploring and hunt for new lands, hoping to survive the treacherous ocean journey. Yeah, it's a comfort game for me.

Andy Edser, Hardware Writer: Crimson Desert is not the ultimate action RPG, despite wearing the ambition proudly on its sleeve. But it's also the most fun I've had in a fantasy open world in years. The map is gigantic, and stuffed with bizarre details to explore. The combat is fiddly, yet satisfying to master. It's a game with obvious passion running underneath it, and a brilliant, bat-swinging attempt to make something with real scope and fresh ideas. More of this sort of thing, please.

Harvey Randall, Staff Writer: Perhaps a bit of a late entrant to catch PC Gamer's eye—which means I don't resent its absence from our Top 100 list—but I absolutely loved Mina the Hollower. It's a sprawling, satisfying Zelda-like with a bumping soundtrack and some of the best exploration I've had in a videogame. I was particularly impressed by how intuitive this game was. My experimentation-loving brain was constantly rewarded for putting its control scheme together in novel ways. Cute little mouse versus the eldritch horrors, what's not to love.

Fraser Brown, Online Editor: Big Walk launched after we created the magazine version of the Top 100 this year, otherwise I know it would have been in the list. This is simply the perfect co-op game. A simple, joyful puzzler absent a single flaw. Some of the antics its puzzles inspired genuinely left my crying with laughter, and that ending? Wow. It's a pure delight, start to finish. It's easily going to be my GOTY for 2026.

Phil has been writing for PC Gamer for nearly a decade, starting out as a freelance writer covering everything from free games to MMOs. He eventually joined full-time as a news writer, before moving to the magazine to review immersive sims, RPGs and Hitman games. Now he leads PC Gamer's UK team, but still sometimes finds the time to write about his ongoing obsessions with Destiny 2, GTA Online and Apex Legends. When he's not levelling up battle passes, he's checking out the latest tactics game or dipping back into Guild Wars 2. He's largely responsible for the whole Tub Geralt thing, but still isn't sorry.

#3774. Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has much worse input lag than PS5

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has noticeably worse input lag than on PS5, which could put Nintendo players at a disadvantage in multiplayer.

Digital Foundry's tech review measured multiplayer latency at 81ms when docked and an average of 100ms in portable mode, against 49ms on PS5. Testing used wireless controllers on both consoles (a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a DualSense), and portable results ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst.

Digital Foundry said "responsiveness here simply isn't as good as on other consoles", and described the lag in portable mode as "actually deleterious to performance" (thanks, IGN).

Beyond the lag, Digital Foundry is fairly positive about the port. Multiplayer runs at 60fps most of the time, and if your TV supports VRR, you'll notice the drops less. The campaign is capped at 30fps and resolution is dynamic.

Docked with DLSS on, the game targets 900p, but Digital Foundry saw it drop to 450p in busier scenes, such as the Paris vehicle chase. In portable mode, the target is 720p, with drops to 360p.

It's been 13 years since a Call of Duty game last appeared on Nintendo hardware, with Ghosts on Wii U in 2013. The series' return is the result of a 10-year deal Microsoft offered Nintendo while it sought regulatory approval for its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

Yesterday we reported that Activision has apologised to the bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it will remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

#3773. Discord has gift cards now, so you can buy Nitro for your ‘online sweetheart’ at retail stores

If you’re looking to spruce up your online appearance with your gaming homies or your long distance relationship but don’t want to enter credit card info online, you’re in luck.

Discord announced today that physical gift cards are coming to retailers across the US, Canada, the UK, France, Italy, and Spain, “making it even easier to give your friends something they’ll actually love on Discord.”

“A gift card makes it easy to buy all sorts of stuff on Discord,” the company said in a new blog post. “Whether you buy one for a friend, your duo partner in your game-night server, or yourself, it’s a direct way to give someone the choice of what to buy on Discord. You choose the amount, and they choose how to spend it.”

If you’re not in the know, Discord is an online chat app that has a subscription called Nitro that gives perks like special customization options, but also bigger upload limits, the ability to stream in 4K, boosts for servers, and more. But you can also purchase customization items like profile effects, nameplates, and more on the app to differentiate yourself however you like.

In the past, you’d need to link a credit card to make purchases, but gift cards add an extra step and a layer of protection if you don’t want to give up your personal info (whatever’s not already out there) to Discord or any other company.

I may or may not have gotten some profile customization skins in the past, so it’s good to know the gift card option is here if you want to snazz yourself up or even give the gift of Nitro to one of your online pals with ease.

Discord says their gift cards can be found at Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and GameStop in the US, and will be rolling out to Micromania in France, Gamelife in Italy, and GAME in Spain.

#3772. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

In yet another example of GTA 6's advanced realism, Rockstar says it features a dynamic weather system that you'll want to navigate carefully lest you find yourself 30,000 feet in the air as a hurricane circles around you.

Talking to Edge for its huge GTA 6 cover story, Rockstar co-studio head Aaron Garbut describes the weather system in GTA 6 as "much more granular" compared to other games where "generally speaking, it's either rainy or sunny or whatever."

I'm not one teeny tiny bit surprised to hear GTA 6 is raising the bar when it comes to in-game weather systems. It is the most expensive game ever made, after all, and Rockstar is well-known for pushing technological boundaries. And yet, I still can't help but feel a childlike excitement at the idea of entire cloud systems moving around independently from each other, of storms that form in the far-off distance and gradually move into town, of surfaces that dry at different speeds after storms. It's stuff like this that contributes to the living, breathing worlds Rockstar is beloved for creating, and with leaps in hardware capabilities every generation, it's always exciting to see what's been made possible.

Speaking of which, wind in GTA 6 sounds genuinely incredible. Garbut says wind will move through Vice City and cause trees to sway and waves to form in water, which would be pretty underwhelming if that was the extent of it, but no, islands and buildings will intercept the force of wind as it does in real life and change the way an anchored boat might bob and sway as it floats along a shoreline. Even your position from within your boat will impact the way waves rock you about.

"Depending on where you are in your boat," Garbut says, "you'll skip over that stuff or get really rocked around by it." Flying a plane or helicopter through the sky on a stormy day or night can also be a risky affair, as severe weather will cause turbulence and potentially cause light damage if you're in the storm for too long. Citizens of Leonida will also seek shelter when severe weather passes through, which definitely feels distinctly Florida. "Everything comes down to these granular levels," Garbut says, "and then it just interacts."

GTA 6 is set to rock the boat on November 19.

GTA 6 lets you break up Jason and Lucia if you want, and we can thank Red Dead Redemption 2's Arthur Morgan for the choice

Baggy Cat Games, the team behind viral FMV horror game At Dead Of Night, has confirmed that a sequel is "coming (very) soon".

At Dead Of Night 2: The Great Hugo picks up where the original game left off and reunites us with Maya as she heads off to investigate a large Tudor manor house.

At Dead Of Night became famous quickly during the pandemic thanks to streamers and content creators like Markiplier, 8-BitRyan, John Wolfe, and DomPlays, who introduced us to Jimmy Hall, a creepy hotel landlord hellbent on recruiting an audience for his late-night comedy show and psychopathic comedy alter ego, Hugo Punch.

The new game, subtitled The Great Hugo, picks up half a decade later.

"Five years later, Maya is still haunted by her experiences in Sea View Hotel," the blurb teases. "Desperate for answers she remembers the ghost box she used in the hotel, left there when she escaped.

"After searching on [auction] sites and in antique shops, she finds a similar looking device, but can’t get it to work. She contacts an old friend and counsellor, Quinn, who had helped her understand her supernatural experiences in the hotel. Quinn recognises the device and knows where they were made - by an inventor who used to live in a large Tudor manor house not far from Sea View - but warns her against trying to get it working. However, Maya ignores his advice and goes on her own investigation."

Quite how long "(very) soon" is, we don't yet know, but we'll keep you posted.

#3768. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

The long-awaited title of the next Elder Scrolls game was revealed in a video marking Bethesda Softworks' 40th anniversary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eight years after it was announced, it's finally officially official: The next RPG in Bethesda's long-running Elder Scrolls series is called Sentinel.

The title was revealed in a video celebrating Bethesda's 40th anniversary, narrated by Todd Howard (of course), who cast back to the studio's first game, Gridiron—Bethesda was big on sports games back in the day—before moving into The Elder Scrolls series, the games that would take it to the big leagues, in the early 1990s.

"As we're here in the 40th anniversary, we think about all of the games we've made," Howard says as the video draws to an end.

"And so even though yes, we're looking back,we're also looking forward to all we're doing, particularly with the Fallout franchise and obviously The Elder Scrolls. You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6. And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."

And thus is the title revealed: Sentinel.

There's an interesting quote after the title is revealed: "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." Those words were uttered by Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell in the year 4E 206, which was UESP pointed out puts Sentinel at least five years after the events of Skyrim.

No other details are revealed, but the title (and that quote) presumably also reveals the setting: Hammerfell, home of the redguards. Sentinel itself is one of Hammerfell's major kingdoms and capital of the Alik'r Desert—reflected in the teaser's sandy backdrop. It's something of a geographical shift from the flyover of the generic mountains seen in that 2018 reveal, although the Alik'r is bordered by the Dragontail Mountains, so who knows.

So there you have it! The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Hopefully it won't take another eight years before we hear anything more about it.

#3766. Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, selling over 4 million copies in three days

Phantom Blade Zero studio S-Game has announced that its debut title has sold more than 4m copies in its first 72 hours on sale. The game's official X account broke the news alongside a celebratory message, though without providing a per-platform breakdown of copies sold.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" the developer wrote on X.

Phantom Blade Zero is available on Steam and PlayStation 5, but the 4m figure also includes sales made on the China-exclusive Tencent WeGame PC launcher. Prior to launch, Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold over 1m copies before it had even released.

It was always clear the third-person character action game was going to be a hit, we just had to wait for actual figures to be released.

Phantom Blade Zero attracted over 431,000 concurrent players on Steam at launch, a figure that kept risking and rising into the weekend, ultimately settling at a massive 833,921 peak concurrent (via SteamDB). Just in case it wasn't already clear, this is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, beating the likes of Forza Horizon 6 and far outpacing all other major releases such as Onimusha: Way of the Sword, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Ace Combat 8.

Despite the very strong opening weekend's numbers, Phantom Blade Zero has not been able to match or exceed the performance of Black Myth: Wukong, 2024's also-Chinese developed triple-A action game, just yet. The breakout hit, estimated to have sold 30m copies since, is one of Steam's largest debuts ever, peaking at 2,415,714 concurrent players at launch.

In Eurogamer's Phantom Blade Zero review, Emma Kent spoke highly of much of the game, but was critical of its underwhelming narrative and lack of consistency, writing: "This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword."

#3764. Soulframe to launch into free open beta this week, as Warframe devs go head-to-head with WoW: Forever

Soulframe's Preludes (its own version of a beta) is finally opening its doors to the whole world ahead of the Verse of the Veilands update. Starting this week, anyone who wants to can simply download the game and hop in, no invite required.

The date this happens is an interesting one: 6th November. That's two days after the release of World of Warcraft: Forever and the same week as Old School RuneScape's Hardcore worlds, so it's suddenly become a pretty packed month for MMO enthusiasts.

This comes after three years of closed testing for the fantasy action MMORPG, which players have been able to gradually see firsthand through sporadic invites. With Soulframe suffering delays since its first reveal, brief invite events have already occurred over this period. Even locked away, the game has received multiple substantial updates over the years, including new quests, Pacts (classes), factions and so on.

As for what newcomers to Soulframe can look forward to when Soulframe opens its doors, the Verse of the Veillands update is bringing a total overhaul of the map progression system this month. After the completion of an early quest, players are introduced to a corrupted landscape, the Veillands, which they must purify.

As you do so, new resources will be obtainable and side activities like fishing will be unlocked. You'll also be able to train up a small wolf pet into a full-on mount in the process. Previously, players were just thrust into the open world to explore and figure things out as they go, so this should provide something of an introduction to the game's open map. It won't be totally finished when released mind you, with updates to the Veillands system coming in the future.

On top of that, there's a new Pact called the Ode Shrike coming with the update. It's a tricksy trapper with spikes, balloon snares, bombs and chains to disrupt enemies as you whittle them down.

Could this be enough to win people over to Digital Extreme's newest project? Time will tell - but in the meantime its long-lasting sci-fi MMO Warframe is taking players to the Tau system in a major next step in the game's narrative this December. It comes with a detective noir inspired main quest, playable warframe, and even an in-universe Poker equivalent.

#3763. WoW Forever Beta Patch Notes (Nov. 3, 2026) – What’s coming before release?

Blizzard dropped one final patch before World of Warcraft: Forever launches.

We’re barely a day and a half away from World of Warcraft: Forever‘s launch, and Blizzard released one last round of patches before our characters re-enter Azeroth for the first time. It’s no bad news, though – everyone is getting a power-up.

This batch of fixes came after some older patches that made the Forever beta feel a bit dull to some players. Blizzard devs admitted that limiting for the sake of balancing was them turning to old habits.

“Some of this round of changes reflects areas where we were likely hasty in turning to Burning Crusade- or Wrath-era solutions rather than carving out new ones that better fit into the Forever combat model,” Community Manager Kaivax said in the patch notes.

Read on below for the biggest changes ahead of WoW: Forever‘s launch day.

Naturally, the newest patch affected WoW Forever classes across the board. But surprisingly, this round of updates weren’t nerfs that kept everyone at the same power levels. That’s old-era stuff, which would defeat the ethos of Forever.

“We came to the realization that trying to hold ourselves roughly to Classic power budgets for each class meant that every new element we added needed to come at the expense of something else,” Kaivax said in the post. “Those reductions left some iconic abilities feeling lackluster, and closed the door to other potentially exciting design options.”

“Our aim in class design is not perfect numerical equality, but rather for every class to feel valuable to the groups they join,” Kaivax added, highlighting the team’s desire to reward players for mastering their class. “In Forever, this is accomplished by doubling down on the strengths and differences that make each class unique, rather than overly unifying them.”

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Blizzard has finally done it – WoW: Forever is fully controller-compatible. You can use the Edit Mode and the Options menu to customize movement, spells, interactions, and a whole host of other options.

The devs also fixed bugs related to keyboard and mouse vis-a-vis gamepad functionality. Expect smoother progress when using the gamepad with action bars, add-ons, inventory, combat, navigation, and the like.

Racial abilities seem to have cut crit bonuses and added buffs to weaker ones.

Everyone’s going to level up during launch, and respawn rates are adjusted to accommodate this. Expect faster respawn rates in starting zones and lowered slowly as you level up. This will be lowered eventually, once the surge settles.

Bags also don’t auto-equip anymore. You have to manually equip them to your chosen slot. And if you dropped the flag in Darkspear Islands, you no longer get a debuff.

See the full list of patch notes in the Blizzard forums.

#3762. "We're doing great," says id Software boss, despite losing "about half of our studio" amid devastating Xbox cuts

Iconic Doom and Quake developer id Software was among the most heavily impacted Microsoft-owned studios during Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating business "reset" earlier this year, with around 136 employees reportedly losing their jobs.

In the wake of those layoffs, id Software co-studio director Marty Stratton was recently asked about the current state of the developer, and how it has been affected by Sharma's cuts. "We're doing great," Stratton told journalists at a recent event (via IGN).

"Not to handwave the [layoffs] away… everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that," he continued. "But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department."

This is not the first time a senior id Software member has pushed back on the narrative the studio has been "nerfed into the ground and gutted". Hugo Martin, id's other co-studio head previously claimed the remaining team is "the size we were when we made Doom 2016, and id Tech is very much alive and well".

Sharma's Xbox reset will ultimately see 3,200 jobs cut across Microsoft's gaming division, with many of those still to come. Those impacted by the first wave of cuts in July, however, included developers working on the id Software's id Tech engine. This is the engine behind all of the studio's games, and is known to be among the most performant engines, consistently producing visually-impressive games that require modest specs to run.

Following the layoffs, many inside and outside the studio said the id Tech team had been gutted. Longtime id Software programmer Chris Hays, who notably wasn't among those let go, said at the time, "It is hard to make a game that is triple-A, that is like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard I mean impossible". Hays also claimed "entire departments" and "entire disciplines" are gone.

While Stratton hasn't addressed those comments directly, he revealed id Software is now "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the modern Wolfenstein games, and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. "We've always had a very close partnership with [MachineGames], but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]," he explained.

"We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead."

Id Software's next project remains unclear. MachineGames, on the other hand, recently said it's not done with Wolfenstein, so it's possible a sequel to 2017's The New Colossus is in the works.

Assassin’s Creed publisher Ubisoft is interested in acquiring the studio behind Dishonored and the in-progress Marvel’s Blade game, according to a new report.

The French connection is there for sure, with the Lyon, France-based Arkane garnering interest from the famously French publisher Ubisoft, so it may be a match made in baguette heaven. Sacre bleu!

A wave of thousands of layoffs has followed at numerous sections of Microsoft, including its gaming divisions and numerous studios within.

I’m sure many will have thoughts about Ubisoft taking on Arkane, with the studio going from one big-budget publisher to another, but if it means that jobs are saved and games continue to get made by people, then for now it could be considered a win if a deal gets made.

I am also quite interested to find out who the other companies looking to bid on Arkane may be, but Bloomberg’s sources could not garner more specific info.

World of Warcraft's big crossover with Dungeons & Dragons is finally here—and despite being a huge flagship collaboration, one of the biggest MMOs meeting with one of the biggest TTRPGs, I'm sad to say I'm feeling just a touch whelmed. This sourcebook is inconsistent—filled with very cool character options in some places, and just pointing at the already-existing player's handbook in others.

That inconsistency doesn't let the whole project down, mind. There are still some rules tucked away in here that I think are great additions to any campaign, not just a World of Warcraft-themed one.

Let's start with the big one: Classes. WoW and D&D do have a lot of overlap in terms of class fantasy—there's not much in the way of appreciable differences between a Fighter and a Warrior, other than a few iconic abilities being missing from the pack. As a result, this rulebook essentially uses the pre-existing classes as a template to throw some WoW flavour on.

Some of these changes are meaningful—take, for example, the Death Knight. This uses the Paladin's chassis, but throws in a ton of impactful changes, replacing Lay on Hands with Death Coil, for example. It also throws a whole new raft of Death Knight-adjacent spells, adjusts your Find Steed with a cool undead ghost that can phase through objects, and more.

A lot of the classes are solved by custom spells like this—the Paladin, for instance, has just the one new subclass to cover for Holy and a bunch of iconic Paladin spells. But the balance of these is a touch skewiff in places. Take Divine Shield, for instance. This thing is straight busted.

It's a 4th level spell, which does admittedly mean you'll only get it at levels 13 plus, but it makes you immune to not only the damage of a triggering attack, but also all damage until the start of your next turn. AND you can't be moved or have your speed reduced. While absolutely correct for the flavour of WoW's iconic bubble, this is crazy overpowered.

And while some of these classes do have a lot new on offer, others are so thin on content it's a wonder why they're there at all. The rogue gets a particularly short end of the stick, for instance. Outlaw rogues are just given a reskinned version of 5e's Swashbuckler subclass (which does, in fairness, have some new Cunning Strike options to bring it up to parity). Otherwise, the book just points you in the direction of pre-existing subclasses.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Others are a complete miss, too. Shamans are all awkwardly stuffed into the chassis of the Barbarian, which only really works for Enhancement shamans—Elemental and Restoration shamans are pretty much just your standard D&D barbarian with some flavour-adjacent rage options, rather than the full spellcasters they are in the videogame.

This inconsistency in quality applies to character origins, too. Some of them have fully bespoke traits—Dracthyr get their visage forms, Void Elves get this cool void form that triggers when you hit identical numbers on an Advantage/Disadvantage roll, and so on. And then there are Orcs and Dwarves, some of WoW's most iconic races, where the book goes: Just use the stuff that's already in the PHB.

And yet, there's a lot to this supplement I actually like. When it's actually adding new options to the classes, I think they're cool—the Frost Mage flavoured feat, Fingers of Frost, gives you extra cold damage against restrained creatures, for example. But the real thing I would encourage you to just crib for your non-Azerothian games are its gathering and crafting systems.

In 5e (and the 2024 rules), crafting's always been sort of a joke. There are tool proficiencies, but they might come up every once in a blue moon. The actual Player's Handbook just says to half the cost of an item, then smacks you around the head with a massive downtime cost for anything particularly expensive—a suit of plate armor takes a whopping 150 days to craft (though you can split this with extra help). At which point you might as well just eat the GP cost and buy the damn thing.

This book, however, has some really neat rules for gathering and crafting professions. Having the right tool proficiency gives you access to a profession, which you can level up when your proficiency bonus increases to new tiers (which also increases the rarity of the items you can make).

Instead of making players shell out the gold cost, these gathering professions have a neat little table for getting enough golds' worth in raw materials to make the thing, with extra bonuses for beating the involved DC by five or more. When you get to higher levels, certain recipes might require items from specific regions—and you might only know how to make those items via recipes obtained from certain factions.

It's still all pretty lightweight (although each profession does have a useful list of suggested recipes it should know) but that's honestly a boon to this system, rather than a bane, because you could very easily just slot this whole mechanic into your homebrew campaign with very little trouble.

And, more to the point, you could very easily make entire adventure hooks out of going to get specific materials for a recipe here—which helps solve D&D crafting's main issue: It's not relevant unless you have literal months of in-game downtime to kill. While the book doesn't make changes to the time-to-craft issue, it's still a major step up.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent."

Renown's another mechanic I like. You get renown with certain factions based on your origins, but you can increase this renown through play to get certain perks. For instance, improved renown with Darnassus gives you the option to learn certain proficiencies, gain a blessing from its leaders, or gather extra materials with herbalism. My favorite of these is the gnomeregan Shield Guardian perk, which specifically states that if you dip below 50 renown again, the guardian turns on you. Sorry buddy, my creator says you dropped off.

Aside from these rules additions, there are also some solid dungeon adventures with their own bespoke stat blocks, extra magic items, and a respectable bestiary full of critters to toss into your campaign.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent—some areas have novel, if a little wonky, additions to the system. Others shrug like the book's designers simply ran out of time and budget, pointing towards resources that you already own.

However, if you are looking to run a WoW-specific campaign, or just want crafting rules that don't suck, it very well might be worth checking out on the strength of its secondary mechanics alone. Just don't go in there expecting a 1:1 replication of the MMORPG. This is still Dungeons & Dragons—and in some places, I mean that literally.

#3757. Over a decade later, Bloodborne remains so popular it reportedly sold a quarter of a million copies this year alone

Bloodborne, FromSoftware's singular Lovecraftian action-RPG, has reportedly sold more than 251,000 copies this year alone.

That's according to Alinea Analytics head of market analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed the figure in a post on X, noting this brings Bloodborne's total sales up to an estimated 10.4m copies, generating $317m (around £236m) in revenue. Elliot also claimed more than half a million people played Bloodborne in October through PlayStation Plus.

Additionally, 12 percent of those are said to have played Elden Ring during the month, while 6 percent played Dark Souls 3, and 5 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. There's a cohort of gamers who are always bouncing between different From[Software] games," Elliott pointed out. "Can't blame them, especially with this one."

Bloodborne is a PlayStation exclusive that sadly never left the PS4, despite consistent calls from fans for ports and remasters. While the game is playable on PS5 through backwards compatibility, Bloodborne barely benefits from the console's advanced hardware, only seeing smoother frame pacing. In other words, it's the same game with barely any perceptible upgrades.

Before Sony closed down Demon's Souls remake developer Bluepoint Games earlier this year, the studio reportedly pitched a Bloodborne remake, but original developer FromSoftware didn't want it to happen. When news of the pitch came to light, former Sony Interactive Entertainment Shuhei Yoshida said Bloodborne has a special place in director Hidetaka Miyazaki's heart and speculated the reason it hasn't had a remake is because Miyazaki would prefer to do it himself but doesn't have the time.

"Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created," Yoshida said at the time. "So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."

#3756. As the controversy around AI-created video game copies continues, Anthropic seemingly restricts Claude's cloning abilities

An update to Anthropic's Claude AI software has seemingly blocked the creation of outright clones or copies of existing games. Instead, Claude has been altered to only create "original" games.

Among the first to share news of the change was X user Chasm, who posted a screenshot showing the new rule, purportedly added around 27th October. "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets," it reads. "Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”.

While Anthropic is yet to issue an official statement on the new rule, technical staff member Addy Osmani commented beneath Chasm's post, confirming the change's legitimacy. He noted it was included because "using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy", but added that creating original games and those built with a user's own assets should still be possible.

Following the new rule's inclusion, users on GitHub shared newfound barriers they'd run into as a result. Reports included being blocked from creating digital modules for board games, and from recreating a commercially produced board game for personal use. Eurogamer has contacted Anthropic for comment on the rule change and its stance on AI game copies.

The modifications to Claude have appeared at a time when AI copies of games have drawn increasing ire, with game communities pushing back against them and developers pulling public-facing demos in fear of having their work stolen. AI-assisted copies of triple-A games have also emerged, including a version of Mario Kart 8 playable in an internet browser. However, this was taken down in a matter of days, presumably thanks to a legal notice from Nintendo.

Of course, even if Claude is prevented from making game copies, other AI tools, such as Deepseek, still lack similar restrictions. Until such measures are ubiquitous, the issue will continue. Given Claude's position as one of the most popular commercial AI tools out there, however, this will certainly make a dent in the problem.

#3755. The Division 2 Y8S3 Red Horizon Climax mission walkthrough

The Climax mission for Y8S3 Red Horizon is now available in The Division 2, and it’s your guaranteed shot to an Exotic. Once unlocked, you can then complete the mission at Master to guarantee yourself the Loaded for Bear Exotic gloves.

Let’s find out how to complete the quest.

To unlock the mission, you have to complete the three Scout challenges in Y8S3 that feature HVTs. You can also complete the remaining Scout weeks, but that’s completely optional. Once unlocked, head to the Washington National Airport to begin the mission.

Wait for the cutscene to play out as Manny will provide you with the starting instructions. Your first task is to help the militia stuck at the clinic. The marker will directly lead you to the room where few militia members are stuck.

Kill all the enemies you find at the location. There will be two waves of enemies, with few elite ones to take down. They will fire at you from all sides, so be careful about incoming damage.

Once you clear all the enemies, your next task is to rendezvous with Avery Miles. Follow the marker to reach Avery and protect the NPC from all incoming damage. There will be several enemies to take down, and they will all primarily focus their shots towards Avery. Your best option is to kill the enemies after intercepting them.

Once the remaining Cleaners are killed, you can proceed to the next step. Follow the marker to reach the Hangar, and there will be plenty of enemies to kill. Since the fight takes place in an open area, use the fence coverings as much as possible.

Once you take care of the cleaners, you’ll need to disable two fuel pumps. The pumps are on either sides of the de-constructed aircraft in the middle. You can just trace them by their pipes. However, focus first on the enemies since that will make things easier for you.

Keep proceeding through the airport and clear the incoming enemies until you get the objective to secure the concourse. Then, reach the tarmac to sabotage the pumps. Keep killing the enemies until the objective marker pops up to disclose the pump locations.

Finally, Bobby Guzman will appear. He is the main enemy of this Climax mission, and he will be a hard challenge. He has plenty of armor on him, and he is surrounded by other elite enemies.

Finally, a timer will commence, giving you approximately a minute to escape. Do so safely, and you’ll successfully finish the Climax mission. You get the guaranteed Exotic drop by playing at Master. Anything less means obtaining the Exotic will be luck-dependent.

#3754. MAGA Clings To Darth Vader As It Braces For Election Results

You do not have to want Democrats to sweep the 2026 election to think that Republicans may have done a historically poor job of trying to appeal to the basic hopes and interests of average voters. The latest evidence we have for that is a bizarre surge in online support among various pockets of MAGA world for Star Wars‘ Anakin Skywalker, AKA Darth Vader.

“Yes, it seems that while the fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) will remain shut down for the foreseeable future, MAGA conservatives are picking up the slack, using the last hours before the 2026 midterms to imagine themselves and Trump-aligned candidates as the disciples of a genocidal archvillain from a space opera,” reported Wired this week.

If you spend any time on X, you may have been exposed to its $865 billion net-worth owner, Elon Musk, sharing genAI slop of what Anakin Skywalker might have done if he’d never been defeated by Obi-Wan Kenobi and left to burn in the lava on Mustafar. “This is what they stole from us,” Musk posted alongside a picture of Anakin and Padme goth’d-out in front of imperial legions and twin Sith in training, Luke and Leia. “Okay Hitler,” reads the top response.

This is what they stole from us pic.twitter.com/q1GnpjF394

While one might expect better shitposts from the richest man in the world, Musk’s MAGA brainrot is noteworthy given the roughly $500 million he spent on this election cycle trying to help get Trump-backed Republicans elected. Can money really buy elections? The ruling elite certainly seems to think so. But everyone knows how very uncool it is to try to astroturf a popularity contest. Anakin is just the latest attempt of a very X-pilled MAGA class to try to make fascism seem cool. Before Anakin it was “Malfoid” fanfic that turned Harry Potter’s pasty, sniveling nepo baby rival into a hot anime school girl.

The Department of Education, which is currently racing to garnish the paychecks of people with student loans in default, recently embraced the Malfoid meme, only to later swap to an Anakin Skywalker variant. “Find the Anakin in your life,” Katie Miller, the wife of Stephen Miller, the Trump deputy chief of staff currently trying to put children in cages, posted on Halloween. “Not surprised to see you idolize the guy who kills kids,” reads the top response.

Still confused? Here’s Axios‘ house-style “smart brevity” bullet points to bring you up to speed:

What they’re saying: Right-wing streamer Kangmin Lee said Anakin represents young men today “who grew up believing the system was fundamentally good, only to discover that the system was never quite what it claimed to be.”

Yes, but: Anakin becomes Darth Vader, a ruthless enforcer of the authoritarian Galactic Empire who murders children, hunts down Jedi Knights and helps terrorize the galaxy.

Be Smart: Go vote. Be kind. A better future is still possible.

Konami might have finally set down the Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol 1 to focus on releasing Metal Gear Solid 4 from its PS3 prison, but modders continue chipping away at the PS2-and-earlier era Metal Gear games. MGSHDFix, whose mission statement is to repair broken visual bugs, fix crashes, and generally give the older Metal Gears a bit of a spitshine, has got a big new update. Now is the era of MGSHDFix 5.0 (actually, 5.0.1. There was a hotfix).

"We've got performance improvements, massive vanilla loading time reductions for MGS2, loose .MP3/.WAV/.OGG/FLAC soundtrack loading for MG1/MG2, WIP raw mouse input support, and loads of new restoration and bugfixes", writes author Afevis Solmunko.

There are, to be honest, way too many fixes to properly delve into here, so I recommend either checking the patch notes out yourself or taking the mod for a spin in your preferred Metal Gear. We can call out some of the big ones, though.

For example, want to play Metal Gear 2 as Mel Gibson? No? Well that's a shame, bucko, because MGSHDFix 5.0 provides an option to restore that game's MSX2 sprites. "Yes, you can finally experience Mel Gibson fighting Sean Connery as Kojima intended," writes Solmunko.

Also in the OG MGs, there's now an option "to make doors automatically check your inventory for keycards (how MGS2 keycards work)", which frankly sounds blasphemous to me.

More practically, the latest version of the mod boasts that it dramatically cuts down loading times in MGS2. "We've greatly sped up level loading by adding a new system that prefetches a list of all the assets for all the rooms that are directly connected to the current stage you're in… Speedrunners have reported that this new prefetch system has shaved upwards to 5 minutes off of the elapsed realtime from their runs". On Linux (and thus, Steam Deck) specifically, Solmunko says this can "reduce level transitions load times by 4~6 seconds for every room you go into".

Plus, MGS2 and MGS3 now have limited support for raw mouse input in third-person, with support for first-person hopefully coming in MGSHDFix 5.1.0.

#3752. One World of Warcraft: Forever player is working on a first-person mod that's a love letter to retro RPGs like Hexen and Morrowind

One World of Warcraft: Forever player is attempting to turn Blizzard's new MMO endeavour into a Morrowind-esque first-person fantasy RPG, full of retro animations harkening back to the good ol' days. And there's no generative AI in sight.

The project, known as Retro Forever, is the work of modder Arhkain, who's so far published two dev vlogs detailing the nature of his work. He opens the first vlog by describing how he always wanted to view the world of Azeroth through his character's eyes, but was met with a lack of adequate options to support this style of play. That encouraged him to find his own solutions, which is how Retro Forever was born.

The result is a WoW Forever mod aiming to incorporate "fully immersive" first-person graphics - whether it be for combat, cooking, or flying across the world - with a presentation style reminiscent of classic first-person fantasy games like Morrowind or Hexen. In fact, the mod currently uses assets pulled and modified from those games.

Retro Forever - which is described as a "clever combination of addons that already exist" - includes a custom user interface, as well as animations attached to specific spells and abilities. That means, if you're a mage and attack an enemy with a spell, you'll see a custom animation of your character doing that spell.

The bad news is the mod isn't publicly available right now, and currently only works with a selection of mage spells and other class abilities. However, that's set to expand - and Arhkain recently revealed an artist has expressed interest in joining the project for original asset creation.

As for the no-generative AI deal, Arhkain said the tool "wouldn't help" in the mod's development. And when Retro Forever has been updated with original art to replace its currently borrowed assets, it should also dodge any legal pitfalls too. Nice!

#3750. Margaret Qualley and Jack Antonoff's Relationship Timeline

Margaret Qualley and Jack Antonoff kept their romance under the radar before getting married.

The twosome were first linked in August 2021 following the Maid star’s brief relationships with Pete Davidson and Shia LaBeouf. The Bleachers singer, for his part, previously dated Lena Dunham from 2012 to 2018.

Nearly two years after Antonoff and Dunham went their separate ways, he was spotted packing on the PDA with Qualley. The Once Upon a Time in Hollywood actress — who is the daughter of Andie MacDowell and Paul Qualley — later joked about the “terrifying” experience of meeting Antonoff’s parents, telling Another magazine in March 2022, “[I thought], ‘Please like me, please like me, this is so important, please.’”

#3749. COD Modern Warfare 4 has seemingly answered DMZ players' PvE calls with new Story Mission changes - but there are major caveats

For as long as Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction mode has been available, there've been calls for PvE-only servers. Developer Infinity Ward, for its part, has maintained the mode is designed as a PvPvE experience, but it's now seemingly made a change offering solo players something of a compromise, albeit with caveats.

In DMZ, your choice of deployment type dictates the matchmaking pool you're put into. You can choose to freely roam the map, picking up tasks as you go, or participate in slightly more structured Dynamic Ops which constantly generate tasks for you to do. But DMZ also has Story Missions, a title that suggests they're private instances. But that wasn't the case at launch. Although the number of players allowed into Story Mission instances appeared to be smaller than in other modes, it was still possible to run into other players, which meant potentially unwanted PvP encounters.

Now, however, Infinity Ward appears to have made Story Missions private, but only for solo players, and only when playing a Story Mission for the first time - after which, repeated attempts will be much less forgiving.

Infinity Ward has not officially announced a change, but players began noticing it on Reddit and elsewhere, and I wanted to investigate for myself: I just finished a Story Mission - a first attempt - and despite making as much noise as possible, I ran into no other players. The Recent Players list in the social tab, which displays the names of players you've recently crossed paths with, was likewise empty for me. I also noticed zero activated UAV Towers and SAM Sites - a rare sight in PvPvE matches where players always run to the former to reveal enemies around them. There's some suggestion you may still run into others in a Story Mission, however, so best not lower your guard. As welcome as the change is, it highlights the split in DMZ's community. Many would rather not cross paths with other players, and it's especially frustrating for those expecting a purely PvE mode in this year's Call of Duty.

#3747. Nintendo tried adding fast travel to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, before devs realised "we were missing out on the moments of discovery"

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version."

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is being wrapped up in all kinds of modern touches for its imminent Nintendo Switch 2 remake (that owl seems to be less chatty, for starters), but there's at least one quality-of-life feature borrowed from Breath of the Wild that the developers felt was better left on the cutting room floor: fast travel.

In Nintendo's latest Ask The Developer blog post, long-time series producer Eiji Aonuma explained that he initially asked the game's remakers to add warp points so players could get around Hyrule without having to spam rolls and presumably make Link violently ill in the process. But he and the team quickly realised fast travel doesn't work so well in a game that's still, in its bones, almost three decades old.

"In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, there are many warp points that enable players to move quickly around the game's vast world. In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry," Aonuma said.

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didn't exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what's this?' Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again."

There you have it. No fast-travel points in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake, and it sounds like it's for the best. I avoided warping around Breath of the Wild's open world for the same reasons Aonuma laid out - spotting something odd way in the distance, slowly finding a way to reach it, and then discovering a funky little Korok seed was always a thrill that wouldn't have been possible by cutting out the trek in between main objectives.

Talking about why Nintendo chose to revive Ocarina of Time now, Aonuma said some of the younger developers on the team had maybe never played the original game 28 years ago, and remaking it could "trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

As for the remake's somewhat divisive art style, art director Aya Shida said the team "used phrases like 'a puppet-show feel' and 'the analog feel of practical effects films'" early on in production. "Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Shida continued.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes out on the 5th of November. After getting some hands-on time with the revival, Lottie thought it was shaping up to be a brilliant remake.

"Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models."

Indie-oriented digital storefront Itch.io is beginning to push back against the rising flood of AI, announcing on social media that it's "deleted a couple terabytes of AI slop" and made it easier for users to filter out games made with generative AI.

A few days after Valve admitted that Steam has a problem with AI slop and game cloning, Itch.io chimed in to say it's experiencing something very similar: The number of game pages being created every day on the storefront has doubled over the past two months.

Itch.io didn't provide a reason for the phenomenon, but it's not hard to figure out: When one Bluesky asked why it was happening, Itch.io replied "take a guess," accompanied by crying and robot smilies, and then added that "the number of downloads and purchases has *not* doubled."

Now it seems to be moving to action. "Just deleted a couple terabytes of AI slop," the storefront posted last night. "Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models."

The account also linked to Itch.io's guidelines on "uploading excessive amounts of automatically generated or AI-generated content," which says that while content created by generative AI "can be useful or interesting, do not use automated systems to mass produce product pages. We will consider this spam and may remove your pages from our browse and search pages."

The guidelines apply to, but are not limited to:

Like Steam, Itch.io requires developers and publishers to disclose their use of generative AI in their games. That disclosure requirement has now been expanded from game assets to "the tabletop (aka physical games), books, comics and soundtracks categories," all of which now require disclosure.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It has also added new browsing and search filters on the site, so users can exclude some or all use of generative AI.

The tabletop (aka physical games), books, comics and soundtracks categories on itchio now require completing an AI disclosure in order to edit or create your page. These join the game assets section which has required disclosure for the past 2 years.

The "No AI" tag page cuts straight to it:

Itch.io's action isn't likely to stem the tide of AI slop that's engulfing the world of gaming. Apart from the fact that it represents a very small percentage of a market dominated by Steam, the simple truth is that AI slop is easy to churn out in overwhelming quantities—that's what makes it so attractive to people who care less about creation than they do about making a few bucks on a lucky swing of the bat.

But it is action, and I think that's important: While some argue that mandatory AI disclosures have the potential to harm developers, the gen AI geyser is unquestionably doing harm right now, to users, developers, and the industry as a whole. Unless and until that changes, proactively excising the worst of the slop torrent and making it easier for gamers to avoid the mess entirely is the least that online storefronts can do.

#3745. Which of Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s Kids Have Changed Their Last Names?

Four of Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s six children have taken steps to remove “Pitt” from their names.

After Jolie filed for divorce from Pitt in September 2016 citing “irreconcilable differences,” Maddox, Zahara, Shiloh and Vivienne have each distanced themselves — publicly or legally — from their famous father by changing their last names. (Jolie and Pitt also share sons Pax and Knox, who have not publicly revealed the same change.)

“[Brad] feels most hurt out of everything that happened with Angie that his children don’t want a public association with his last name,” a source exclusively told Us Weekly in May 2026. “It’s been very difficult.”

Pitt and Jolie ultimately finalized their divorce in December 2024, though the F1 actor still remains estranged from several of his children.

Scroll down to see which of Pitt and Jolie’s kids have changed their last names:

Pitt and Jolie’s daughter Shiloh filed a motion to change her last name on her 18th birthday in May 2024. In court documents obtained by Us, Shiloh requested to drop Pitt and simply go by Shiloh Jolie. Her petition was granted three months later without a hearing.

“[Shiloh] hired her own lawyer and paid for it herself,” a source told Us in June 2024.

A second insider added that Pitt was “devastated by this choice,” explaining, “To him, it was more than a change of name — it was a symbol of a deeper estrangement that has been brewing for years.”

Zahara filed her own petition with the Superior Court of California to legally become Zahara Jolie in April 2026, which was processed that June.

Weeks earlier, she was called “Zahara Marley Jolie” during her Spelman College graduation. Zahara introduced herself the same way in 2023 when joining the Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority, chanting, “My name is Zahara Marley Jolie. Coming all the way from the Golden State in the city that is full of angels, Los Angeles, California. … I am this line’s No. 7.”

A source, meanwhile, dispelled the narrative that Pitt was wounded by Zahara’s decision.

“The children are now adults and make their own decisions,” the insider told Us. “It’s really horrible that [Pitt] has tried to paint himself as a victim. When will people start asking real questions about what happened to the kids?”

In September 2026, Us obtained court documents confirming that a Los Angeles judge officially signed off on Zahara’s request to change her name from “Zahara Marley Jolie-Pitt to Zahara Marley Jolie.”

Judge Virginia Keeny wrote in her ruling, “There being no objections, the petition for change of name is granted. The Decree is signed and filed. The Petitioner’s name is changed from Zahara Marley Jolie-Pitt to Zahara Marley Jolie.”

The hearing was held at the Los Angeles Superior Court’s Stanley Mosk Courthouse, though Zahara was represented virtually by her lawyer Peter Kenneth Levine. (Page Six was the first to report the news.)

Maddox filed his own paperwork in May 2026 to legally become Maddox Chivan Jolie, using his middle name in place of Pitt, Us confirmed. (Jolie adopted Maddox before meeting Pitt, though the actor later became his legal father.)

Months earlier, Maddox was credited simply as “Maddox Jolie” in the end credits of Jolie’s film Couture, where he served as an assistant director.

Vivienne was credited as a production assistant on the Broadway show The Outsiders, which her mother produced, with the Playbill listing her name as Vivienne Jolie.

Us confirmed in July 2026 that Vivienne also filed to drop “Pitt” from her surname. A judge granted her request that November, allowing her to legally change her name to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie.
